children.title: CIA Triad — Confidentiality, Integrity & Availability
children.label: CIA Triad
children.summary: Every security control maps to protecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability.
children.core_idea:
- **Confidentiality** — only authorized parties can read the data (encryption, access control)
- **Integrity** — data hasn't been altered without authorization (hashing, signing, checksums)
- **Availability** — systems/data are accessible when needed (redundancy, DDoS protection, backups)
- Controls often trade off against each other — e.g. strict access control (confidentiality) can slow legitimate access (availability)
- Use the triad to classify *why* a given control exists, not just *what* it does

children.title: Information Assurance — The Four Pillars
children.label: Information Assurance
children.summary: | Pillar | Goal | |---|---| | **Confidentiality** | Information is accessible only to authorized parties | | **Integrity** | Information is accurate and has not been altered without authorization | | **Availability** |…
children.core_idea:
| Pillar | Goal |
|---|---|
| **Confidentiality** | Information is accessible only to authorized parties |
| **Integrity** | Information is accurate and has not been altered without authorization |
| **Availability** | Systems and data are accessible to legitimate users when needed |
| **Policy / Privacy** | Governs how data is handled and who is permitted to access it |

### Networking Realities That Undermine These Pillars
- A vulnerability in a single **application** can take just that app offline; a vulnerability in the **OS** can take down the entire host — the blast radius scales with the layer compromised
- **Addressing is a weak point** — every device needs a MAC address for its local segment, and IP addresses provide global uniqueness at the network layer, but **neither is verified**. An attacker can spoof any source address they choose, which undermines any control that trusts an address as a proxy for identity
- **TCP** is connection-oriented and reliable; **UDP** is connectionless and faster but gives no delivery guarantee — the choice between them is itself a security-relevant design decision (UDP-based protocols are easier to spoof and amplify)
- **Port numbers** identify which application on a host should receive traffic (80 = HTTP, 443 = HTTPS, etc.)

### Devices, By Trust Model
- **Hub** — broadcasts every packet to all connected devices; every machine on the segment can see all traffic (bad for confidentiality)
- **Switch** — forwards frames only to the intended destination
- **Router** — connects networks, forwarding based on destination IP and routing-table metrics; routers only need to know what their immediate neighbors can reach, not the full topology of the internet

children.title: Defense in Depth — Layered Security Controls
children.label: Defense in Depth
children.summary: Stack multiple, independent controls so no single failure exposes the whole system.
children.core_idea:
- No single control is assumed perfect — layer network, host, application, and data-level defenses
- If one layer fails (e.g. firewall misconfigured), the next layer (e.g. host-based EDR) should still catch the attacker
- Applies vertically (network → host → app → data) and horizontally (multiple controls at the same layer)
- Classic real-world failure: relying on the perimeter firewall alone and having nothing internal to catch lateral movement

children.title: Zero Trust — Never Trust, Always Verify
children.label: Zero Trust
children.summary: Assume no user, device, or network segment is trustworthy by default — verify every request explicitly.
children.core_idea:
- Replaces the old "trusted internal network / untrusted internet" perimeter model — internal traffic is verified too
- Core pillars: verify identity explicitly, use least-privilege access, assume breach (segment and monitor as if the attacker is already inside)
- Requires strong identity (MFA), device posture checks, and micro-segmentation — not just a VPN at the edge
- Common misconception: Zero Trust is an architecture/strategy, not a single product you buy

children.title: Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact
children.label: Risk Formula
children.summary: Practical risk depends on valuable assets, realistic threats, exploitable weaknesses, and likely impact.
children.core_idea:
- Asset: what has value (systems, data, credentials, reputation).
- Threat: actor or condition capable of causing loss.
- Vulnerability: exploitable weakness in design, config, or process.
- Probability and impact together determine practical priority.
- A vulnerability without credible threat exposure is not always top risk.

children.title: Core Security Vocabulary — Vulnerability, Threat, Attack, Risk
children.label: Core Security Vocabulary
children.summary: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is potential harm; an attack is a threat carried out — precise vocabulary that underlies every policy and risk discussion.
children.core_idea:
### Definitions
- **Vulnerability** — a weakness that, if exploited, compromises one of the CIA properties:
  - Corrupted → loss of **integrity** (the asset no longer does its intended function correctly)
  - Leaky → loss of **confidentiality** (information is disclosed to unauthorized parties)
  - Unavailable/very slow → loss of **availability** (legitimate users can't access the asset)
- **Threat** — the *potential* for a security harm to an asset; not yet realized
- **Attack** — a threat that has been **carried out**, leading to an actual violation of security policy
  - **Passive attack** — attempts to learn or make use of information from a system without affecting its state (e.g. eavesdropping)
  - **Active attack** — attempts to alter system state or resources (e.g. modifying data, denial of service)
- **Security Policy** — the set of rules and regulations specifying how an organization protects its assets; vulnerabilities, threats, and attacks are all defined relative to violating this policy

### Why This Matters
Precise terminology avoids conflating "we have a vulnerability" (a weakness exists) with "we're under attack" (someone is actively exploiting it) — risk communication and incident response both depend on keeping these distinct.

children.title: Threat Actor Sophistication & Organization
children.label: Threat Actor Sophistication &
children.summary: Attackers range from script kiddies using off-the-shelf tools to state-sponsored APTs that patiently target specific high-value organizations.
children.core_idea:
### Levels of Expertise
| Level | Description |
|---|---|
| **Script Kiddie** | Minimal technical skill, uses existing off-the-shelf tools — comprises the largest share of attackers and is the easiest category to defend against |
| **Amateur** | Some real skill, often opportunistic rather than targeted |
| **Professional / APT** | Skilled, well-resourced, and targeted — see below |

### Organizational Structure
Individual actor → cause-based group → loose collective (e.g. hacktivist groups) → organized criminal enterprise (run like a business) → state-based actor, which itself splits into **state-supported**, **state-sponsored**, and **state-run** operations depending on how directly the government controls it.

### Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)
- Selects specific, high-value targets and waits patiently for an opening — a misconfiguration, a missed patch — rather than opportunistically scanning broadly
- Also targets **employees directly** via phishing: credential theft, drive-by malware downloads, malicious attachments
- **Typical APT targets:** critical infrastructure (water, power, transport), financial institutions, and organizations holding valuable IP (agriculture, manufacturing, advanced technology)

### Why Adversaries Prefer Cyber Operations
Compared to physical operations, cyber attacks offer: **reach** (remote, global targeting), **anonymity** (harder to trace, lower legal/physical risk), **cost efficiency** (major disruption for a fraction of the resources), **speed** (exploit before a patch lands), **scalability** (same tooling scales from one victim to an entire nation), and easy **reconnaissance** (scanning, OSINT on employees, data discovery) — combined with modern infrastructure's deep and growing digital dependence.

children.title: Attack Surface — Physical, Network & Third-Party Access Vectors
children.label: Attack Surface
children.summary: Attack surface spans physical access to devices, network-based access, and third-party/insider paths — each split further into deliberate vs. accidental exposure.
children.core_idea:
| Access Type | Mode | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical** | At rest | Accessing a stored device or file directly |
| **Physical** | In motion | Lost laptops, improperly discarded storage media |
| **3rd-Party Physical** | Deliberate | A malicious insider with legitimate physical access |
| **3rd-Party Physical** | Accidental | An untrained insider mishandling sensitive data |
| **Network** | Active | Direct break-in or exploitation |
| **Network** | Passive | Traffic sniffing / eavesdropping |
| **Network** | Social | Using network-based deception to get a third party to expose data themselves |

This framing is useful for threat modeling: for any asset, walk each row and ask whether that specific access mode is realistically open to an attacker, rather than treating "attack surface" as a single undifferentiated blob.

children.title: Adversary Target System Categories
children.label: Adversary Target System Categories
children.summary: Adversaries target data systems, process systems, or control systems — each with a different attack goal and a different worst-case outcome.
children.core_idea:
| System Type | Description | Example Attack |
|---|---|---|
| **Data Systems** | Store critical data — IP, PII, credit card numbers | Ransomware: encrypt and exfiltrate, threaten to publish |
| **Process Systems** | Run essential operations — billing, inventory, medical records | Ransomware: halt operations directly to force a payout |
| **Control Systems** | Manage physical assets — pipelines, power grids, traffic control | Manipulate sensor data or setpoints to cause **physical** damage, not just data loss |

Vulnerable-system root causes cut across all three categories: bad access controls, misconfiguration (both initial setup and later reconfiguration errors), unpatched/legacy systems, and zero-days. Control-system attacks are the highest-consequence category since the "data" being manipulated has direct physical-world effects.

children.title: Security Control Types — Preventive, Detective, Corrective, Compensating
children.label: Control Types
children.summary: Attack categories map to where defenses fail: OS defaults, app flaws, insecure bundled code, and misconfiguration.
children.core_idea:
- Operating system attacks exploit insecure defaults, missing patches, and exposed services.
- Application-level attacks target business logic and unsafe input handling in app code.
- Shrink-wrap code attacks abuse insecure scripts/modules shipped with products.
- Misconfiguration attacks win when convenience settings override hardening.
- Prioritize controls where misconfig + exploitability + impact overlap.

children.title: Principle of Least Privilege
children.label: Least Privilege
children.summary: Grant only the access required to do the job — nothing more, and only for as long as needed.
children.core_idea:
- Every account, service, and process should hold the minimum permissions needed for its function
- Reduces blast radius — a compromised low-privilege account can't pivot as far as an over-privileged one
- Applies to humans (job-role-based access) and to systems (service accounts, API keys, IAM roles)
- Pair with periodic access reviews — permissions creep upward over time unless actively pruned back

children.title: OSI Model & Network Architectures
children.label: OSI Model & Network
children.summary: The OSI model's 7 layers separate concerns from physical bit transmission up through application services; real networks use circuit-, message-, or packet-switching.
children.core_idea:
### The 7 Layers (top to bottom)
| Layer | Transfers | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Application** | — | Services required by end-user applications (closest to the user) |
| **Presentation** | — | Data formatting, encryption, compression |
| **Session** | — | Manages sessions/dialogs between hosts |
| **Transport** | Segments | End-to-end delivery — reliable stream (TCP: handshake, flow control, congestion control) or fast unreliable datagrams (UDP) |
| **Network** | Packets | Routing, addressing (IP) |
| **Data Link** | Frames | Error detection (CRC), flow control *(no congestion control — that's an end-to-end concept)*, Medium Access Control for shared LANs |
| **Physical** | Bits | Raw signal transmission |

### Network Architectures & Transfer Modes
- **Circuit switching** ("reserve and use") — automated switches establish a dedicated physical path for the whole call; classic telephone network
- **Message switching** ("store and forward") — telegraph-style; whole messages hop node to node
- **Packet switching** ("break and route") — modern internet; messages are broken into packets, each independently routed and reassembled at the destination

### Features of the Internet
A digital, global, packet-switched network of networks (WANs/LANs), organized as a layered architecture (OSI vs. the simpler TCP/IP 4-layer model in practice).

children.title: Physical Layer — Line Coding Schemes
children.label: Physical Layer
children.summary: Line coding maps bits to physical signal levels; schemes trade off DC balance, clock recovery, and noise immunity differently.
children.core_idea:
Good line coding needs: **timing recovery**, low implementation complexity/cost, low power, noise immunity, and ideally built-in error detection.

| Scheme | Mapping | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|
| **Unipolar NRZ** | `1`→+A, `0`→0 | Simple but poor timing recovery, has a DC component |
| **Polar NRZ** | `1`→+A/2, `0`→−A/2 | Simple, energy efficient, better noise immunity — still poor timing recovery |
| **Bipolar** | `1` alternates +A/2/−A/2, `0`→0 | Zero DC component; long runs of zeros still lose sync (fixed with B8ZS/B6ZS/B3ZS substitution codes) |
| **Manchester (1B2B)** | `1`→+A/2→−A/2, `0`→−A/2→+A/2 (transition mid-bit) | Self-clocking, excellent timing recovery; coding rate is only 1/2 bit per pulse (10 Mbps needs 20 MHz baud) |
| **mBnL** | m bits → n pulses over L signal levels, constrained by 2^m ≤ Lⁿ | Coding rate = m/n; examples: 2B1Q (2²≤4¹), 4B3T (2⁴≤3³) |
| **NRZI** | `1`→transition at bit start, `0`→no transition | Differential (polarity-insensitive); errors tend to occur in pairs |
| **Differential Manchester** | `1`→no transition at start, `0`→transition at start, always a mid-bit transition | Polarity insensitive, excellent clock recovery, errors occur in pairs. Unlike plain Manchester, it's robust to accidental polarity inversion (+/− swapped) |

### Noise & Reliable Communication
- Noise limits amplitude-detection accuracy, restricts usable signal levels, and raises **Bit Error Rate (BER)**
- **SNR** = Average Signal Power / Average Noise Power; larger SNR → lower BER. In decibels: `SNR(dB) = 10·log₁₀(SNR)`

### Shannon Channel Capacity
```
C = W · log₂(1 + SNR)   bps
```
where `W` = bandwidth (Hz). If the desired rate `R ≤ C`, arbitrarily reliable communication is achievable with sufficiently complex coding (BER can be made arbitrarily small); if `R > C`, reliable communication is **not possible** regardless of coding.

children.title: Ethernet — IEEE 802.3 MAC Frame Structure
children.label: Ethernet
children.summary: Frame = Preamble + addresses + Length + payload + Pad + FCS; switches replaced hubs by giving each port its own collision domain.
children.core_idea:
- Frame layout: 7B Preamble, 1B Start Delimiter, 6B+6B Dest/Src MAC, 2B Length, variable payload (46–1500B), variable Pad (to 64B minimum), 4B FCS (CRC-32 check)
- **Hub** — broadcasts every frame to all ports, one shared collision domain. **Switch** — forwards only to the correct port by MAC, separate collision domain per port — why switches replaced hubs
- Standards scaled from 10Base5 (thick coax, bus) → 10BaseT (twisted pair, star) → Fast/Gigabit/10G Ethernet, still the dominant LAN standard

children.title: Medium Access Control — ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD
children.label: Medium Access Control
children.summary: Random-access MAC protocols coordinate loosely: ALOHA just sends and retries, CSMA senses the channel first, and CSMA/CD aborts early on collision to save bandwidth.
children.core_idea:
### Two Broad Approaches to Sharing a Medium
- **Static Channelization** — fixed, dedicated channels per user (used in satellite/cellular)
- **Dynamic Medium Access Control** — channels allocated on demand, either via **Scheduling** (coordinated, e.g. Token Ring) or **Random Access** (loose coordination — send, wait, retry)

### ALOHA
The simplest random-access scheme: transmit whenever you have data, retry on collision. The conceptual basis for CSMA and its descendants.

### CSMA (Carrier Sensing Multiple Access)
A station senses the channel before transmitting:
- **Idle** → transmit immediately
- **Busy** → wait, per variant:
  - **1-Persistent** — keep sensing, transmit the instant it goes idle (aggressive, high collision risk with multiple waiting stations)
  - **Non-Persistent** — wait a random backoff before sensing again (less aggressive, lower utilization, fewer collisions)

### CSMA/CD (Collision Detection)
Improves on CSMA by **aborting transmission immediately** on detecting a collision, instead of wasting bandwidth sending a doomed frame to completion:
1. Detect collision mid-transmission
2. Abort
3. Send a short **jamming signal** so all stations know a collision occurred
4. Apply a backoff algorithm before re-attempting

### Interconnection Devices by Layer
| Device | Layer | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Repeater | Physical (L1) | Amplifies/regenerates signal |
| Switch/Bridge | Data Link (L2) | Forwards frames by MAC address |
| Router | Network (L3) | Routes packets by IP address |
| Gateway | L4+ | Translates between different protocols/architectures |

children.title: Error Detection & Recovery — CRC and ARQ
children.label: Error Detection & Recovery
children.summary: CRC appends check bits computed via polynomial division to detect transmission errors; ARQ protocols use ACK/NAK, retransmission, and sequence numbers to recover from them.
children.core_idea:
### CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)
Given `k` information bits, CRC generates `n − k` check bits by polynomial division, producing an `n`-bit codeword:
1. Represent the `k` info bits as an information polynomial `i(x)`
2. Multiply by `x^(n-k)` to make room for check bits, forming the dividend polynomial
3. Divide by a fixed generator polynomial `g(x)` (the divisor) using modulo-2 (XOR) arithmetic
4. The remainder becomes the check bits, appended to form the codeword polynomial
5. Transmit the resulting `n`-bit codeword
6. Receiver divides the received codeword by the same `g(x)` — a non-zero remainder means an error was detected

CRC can be implemented efficiently in hardware using a **shift register circuit** wired to perform the polynomial division on the fly.

### Error Vector & Undetectable Errors
`received = codeword XOR error_vector`. A CRC can only detect the error if the error polynomial isn't itself a multiple of the generator polynomial — this is why **certain even-numbered bit-error patterns**, and error bursts longer than the generator's degree, can occasionally slip through undetected. **FUE (Fraction of Undetectable Errors)** quantifies this residual risk for a given burst length `L`.

### ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest)
Three design goals for a working ARQ protocol:
1. Deliver each frame **error-free**
2. Deliver each frame **exactly once** (no duplicates)
3. Deliver frames **in order**

Five basic elements: (1) error detection via CRC, (2) control frames — ACK required, NAK optional, (3) retransmission, (4) timeout, (5) sequence numbers.

**Cumulative acknowledgment:** `ACK(20)` means every frame with sequence number < 20 has been received correctly, and frame #20 is the next one the receiver expects.

children.title: IP Subnetting — Masks, CIDR & Longest Prefix Match
children.label: IP Subnetting
children.summary: Subnetting borrows host-ID bits to create smaller networks; the subnet address is the bitwise AND of the IP and mask, and routers use longest-prefix match when multiple entries match.
children.core_idea:
### Core Formula
```
subnet address = IP address  AND  subnet mask
```

### Worked Example — Class B, need ≤100 hosts/subnet
Given network `150.100.0.0/16`, split into subnets of up to 100 hosts each:
- Need 7 host-ID bits → 2⁷ − 2 = **126 usable hosts** (comfortably covers 100)
- Remaining 16 − 7 = **9 bits** for subnet ID → up to 512 subnets, mask = `/25` = `255.255.255.128`

Find the subnet containing `150.100.12.176`:
```
IP:   10010110 01100100 00001100 10110000
Mask: 11111111 11111111 11111111 10000000   (/25)
AND:  10010110 01100100 00001100 10000000   = 150.100.12.128
```
- Directed broadcast: `150.100.12.255` (all host bits set to 1)
- Usable range: `150.100.12.129`–`150.100.12.254` (2⁷ − 2 = 126 hosts)

### Variable-Length Subnetting
Different departments can get different-sized subnets from the same block — e.g. from `195.100.20.0/24` (Class C): a 90-host department gets a `/25`, and two 60-host departments each get a `/26`. Subnets must never overlap; if remaining address space is oddly shaped, a department may need multiple smaller subnets rather than one contiguous block.

### Longest Prefix Match
When a packet's destination matches multiple routing table entries, the router picks the entry with the **most specific (longest) prefix**:
```
Dest         Mask   Next-hop
150.100.0.0   /16    R1
150.100.12.128 /25   R2

Packet to 150.100.12.176 matches both → routed via R2 (/25 wins over /16)
```

### Real-World Example (`10.24.101.130`, mask `/22`)
```
IP:   00001010 00011000 01100101 10000010
Mask: 11111111 11111111 11111100 00000000
AND:  00001010 00011000 01100100 00000000  = 10.24.100.0/22
```
Usable range: `10.24.100.1`–`10.24.103.254` (2¹⁰ − 2 = 1022 hosts).

children.title: Routing Protocols — RIP, OSPF, BGP & Autonomous Systems
children.label: Routing Protocols
children.summary: An Autonomous System is a network under one administrative domain; interior protocols (RIP, OSPF) route within it, BGP routes between AS's.
children.core_idea:
### Autonomous Systems (AS)
A network (or group of networks) under a single administrative authority, identified by an AS number.
- **Stub AS** — connects to only one other AS (e.g. a single-homed business)
- **Multi-homed AS** — connects to multiple AS's but doesn't relay transit traffic between them
- **Transit AS** — connects multiple AS's and carries traffic on their behalf (ISP backbones)

### IGP vs EGP
- **IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol)** — routes within a single AS. Examples: RIP, OSPF
- **EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol)** — routes between AS's. Example: BGP

### RIP (Routing Information Protocol)
- **Distance-Vector** algorithm — each router shares its routing table with neighbors
- Runs over **UDP port 520**
- Metric = hop count, **max 15 hops**; **16 = infinity (unreachable)** — this caps RIP to small networks
- Vulnerable to routing loops; mitigated with **Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse**

### OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)
- **Link-State** algorithm — each router builds a full map of the network topology and runs Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm locally
- Runs directly over IP (protocol field = 89), not over TCP/UDP
- Converges faster and scales better than RIP; standard choice for interior routing in larger networks

### BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)
- **Path-Vector** algorithm — the protocol of the internet backbone, routes between AS's
- Runs over **TCP** (port 179) for reliable session establishment
- Policy-based, not purely shortest-path — routing decisions incorporate business relationships and administrative policy, not just path length

children.title: Distance-Vector Routing Loops & Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse
children.label: Distance
children.summary: Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse stops 2-node routing loops by reporting ∞ back to where a route came from.
children.core_idea:
- Distance-vector protocols (e.g. RIP) can form routing loops ("counting to infinity") when a link fails and neighbors keep advertising stale routes to each other
- **SHPR rule**: if node W routes to Y *through* X, W tells X specifically that its distance to Y is ∞ — even though W's real distance may not be
- This stops X from routing back through W after a failure, since W is (correctly, from X's view) saying "I don't have an independent route"
- **Limitation**: SHPR only fixes loops between exactly two nodes — loops spanning 3+ nodes still require counting to infinity (bounded by RIP's 16-hop limit)

children.title: NAT — Network Address Translation
children.label: NAT
children.summary: NAT lets many private hosts share one public IP by rewriting the (IP, port) pair on outbound packets and maintaining a translation table to route replies back.
children.core_idea:
### Purpose
Converts between **private** and **global** IP addresses so multiple private hosts can share one public IP.

### Operation
- Internal hosts generate packets with **private IP + TCP/UDP port**
- The NAT router maps each **(private IP, port)** pair to a **(shared public IP, available port)** pair, recording the mapping in an **Address Translation Table**
- Return traffic is matched against the table and routed back to the correct internal host

```
Private Network              NAT Router                Public Network
192.168.0.10 : x   ──►   Address Translation   ──►   128.100.10.15 : y
192.168.0.13 : w   ──►         Table            ──►   128.100.10.15 : z
```

### Security Implication
NAT incidentally provides a thin layer of obscurity — internal hosts aren't directly addressable from the internet — but it is **not** a substitute for a firewall; it doesn't inspect or filter traffic content.

children.title: TCP Segment Header & Control Bits
children.label: TCP Segment Header &
children.summary: TCP flags and header fields drive connection state, scan behavior, and many detection signatures.
children.core_idea:
- SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, and URG indicate connection intent and transitions.
- Port fields map traffic to services and attack targets.
- Sequence and acknowledgment numbers support session integrity and analysis.
- Flag combinations power scan methods and IDS detection logic.
- Malformed or unusual header patterns can indicate probing or evasion.

children.title: TCP Connection Lifecycle — Handshake, Teardown, SYN Flood
children.label: TCP Connection Lifecycle
children.summary: Understanding handshake and teardown states is core to detecting scans, resets, and session abuse.
children.core_idea:
- Three-way handshake establishes synchronized state before payload transfer.
- FIN/RST behavior affects teardown semantics and detection fidelity.
- SYN-heavy patterns can indicate scanning or DoS pressure.
- State tracking helps separate normal retransmits from suspicious retries.
- Connection lifecycle anomalies are high-value signals in network monitoring.

children.title: TCP RTO Estimation — Karn's & Jacobson's Algorithms
children.label: TCP RTO Estimation
children.summary: Accurately estimating the retransmission timeout requires solving ACK ambiguity (Karn's Algorithm) and accounting for RTT variance (Jacobson's Algorithm).
children.core_idea:
### Problem 1 — ACK Ambiguity
When a segment is retransmitted, an incoming ACK is ambiguous: is it acknowledging the original transmission or the retransmission? Assuming the wrong one skews the RTT estimate (too large or too small either way).

**Karn's Algorithm:**
1. Only update `RTT_EST` using samples from segments that were **not** retransmitted
2. Ignore RTT samples that involve any retransmitted segment
3. To avoid the RTO staying too small under sustained loss, **double the RTO on each retransmission**: `RTO = γ × RTO` (γ typically 2)
4. Keep doubling until a valid (non-retransmitted) sample arrives, then recompute RTO normally from the fresh `RTT_EST`

### Problem 2 — High Variance in RTT
A simple exponential moving average (`RTT_EST = α·RTT_EST + (1−α)·RTT_Sample`) captures the mean but ignores variance. Real RTT distributions have heavy tails, so a fixed multiple of the mean (e.g. `RTO = 2 × RTT_EST`) causes frequent spurious timeouts.

**Jacobson's Algorithm** tracks the mean **and** the deviation:
```
D_Sample = |RTT_EST − RTT_Sample|
RTT_EST  = 7/8 × RTT_EST + 1/8 × RTT_Sample     (α = 0.875)
D_EST    = 3/4 × D_EST   + 1/4 × D_Sample        (δ = 0.75)
RTO      = RTT_EST + 4 × D_EST                    (η = 4)
```
This replaces the naive `RTO = 2 × RTT_EST` with a variance-aware formula, dramatically reducing unnecessary retransmissions on high-jitter paths.

children.title: TCP Congestion Control — cwnd, Slow Start & Congestion Avoidance
children.label: TCP Congestion Control
children.summary: TCP probes for available bandwidth with an exponentially-growing congestion window (Slow Start), then switches to linear growth (Congestion Avoidance) once near capacity.
children.core_idea:
### Core Mechanism
TCP maintains a **congestion window (cwnd)** limiting how much unacknowledged data it can have in flight, separate from the receiver's flow-control window (**rwnd**). The actual send window is `swnd = min(rwnd, cwnd)`.

TCP has no direct visibility into network congestion, so it infers it indirectly: **packet loss is treated as a congestion signal**.

### Phase 1 — Slow Start (SS)
- `cwnd` starts at 1 MSS (default MSS often 536 bytes historically; commonly ~1460 bytes on modern Ethernet paths)
- Every RTT with no loss, `cwnd` **doubles** (exponential growth) — one MSS added per received ACK
- Continues until `cwnd` reaches **ssthresh** (slow-start threshold), at which point TCP switches to Congestion Avoidance

### Phase 2 — Congestion Avoidance (CA)
- Entered when `cwnd ≥ ssthresh`
- Each non-duplicate ACK: `cwnd ← cwnd + 1/⌊cwnd⌋` — net effect is **cwnd grows by ~1 MSS per RTT** (linear/additive growth)

```
cwnd
 ▲                          ssthresh
 │                    ┌───── (CA: +1/RTT, linear)
 │             ┌─────/
 │      ┌─────/
 │ ┌───/     (SS: doubles each RTT)
 │/
 └──────────────────────────────► time
```

A real capture typically shows this visually: a sharp exponential spike during Slow Start, followed by a "staircase" of small linear increments during Congestion Avoidance, with occasional sawtooth drops on loss events.

### Detecting Congestion
Congestion is inferred from either:
- **Timeout (RTO expiry)** — a strong congestion signal, treated aggressively
- **Triple duplicate ACK** — a weaker/faster signal that a single segment was lost, handled less aggressively (Fast Retransmit) since later segments are still arriving fine

children.title: TCP Congestion Control Variants — Tahoe, Reno, Vegas, CUBIC, BBR
children.label: TCP Congestion Control Variants
children.summary: Successive TCP variants respond to loss less destructively (Tahoe → Reno → CUBIC) or shift from loss-based to delay-based congestion signals (Vegas, BBR).
children.core_idea:
| Variant | Congestion Response | Key Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Tahoe** | Any loss (timeout *or* dup ACK) → `cwnd = 1`, `ssthresh = cwnd/2`, restart Slow Start | Simple but destroys throughput on every single loss |
| **Reno** | Distinguishes RTO (full Tahoe-style reset) from triple-dup-ACK (**Fast Recovery**: halve cwnd and continue from there instead of dropping to 1) | Avoids over-reacting to isolated packet loss |
| **New Reno** | Improves Reno's Fast Recovery to correctly handle **partial ACKs** — multiple losses in one window no longer prematurely exit Fast Recovery | Better behavior under multiple losses per RTT |
| **Vegas** | Delay-based — compares actual throughput to expected throughput; increases/decreases cwnd based on how many packets appear to be queuing, *before* loss occurs | Proactive rather than reactive to congestion |
| **CUBIC** | Loss-based but backs off less aggressively (~20% cwnd cut vs. 50%) and grows cwnd along a cubic function of time since the last loss | Default on Linux; designed for high-bandwidth, high-latency ("long fat") networks |
| **BBR** | Model-based — estimates bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation delay directly, then paces sending to match, rather than reacting to loss at all | Google's algorithm; avoids filling buffers (bufferbloat) that loss-based algorithms tolerate |

**Classification:** packet-loss-based algorithms (Tahoe/Reno/New Reno/CUBIC) treat loss as the congestion signal; delay-based algorithms (Vegas, BBR) watch for increasing latency as an earlier warning sign, aiming to avoid loss altogether rather than recover from it.

children.title: Socket Programming — TCP/UDP Basics (C / BSD sockets)
children.label: Socket Programming
children.summary: Client-server socket programs share a common structure: create a socket, address it, then either connect (TCP client) / bind+listen+accept (TCP server) before exchanging data.
children.core_idea:
### Roles
- **Client** — initiates a connection; needs the server's IP address and port
- **Server** — waits for connections on a known port; once a client connects, the server has the client's IP + port too

### Creating a Socket
```c
int socket(int domain, int type, int protocol);
```
- `domain` — communication domain, `PF_INET` for IPv4
- `type` — `SOCK_STREAM` for TCP, `SOCK_DGRAM` for UDP
- `protocol` — usually `0` (let the OS pick based on type)
- Returns a socket descriptor (int) on success, `-1` on failure

### Addressing — `struct sockaddr_in`
```c
struct sockaddr_in addr;
addr.sin_family      = PF_INET;
addr.sin_port        = htons(portNum);      // host-to-network byte order
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = inet_addr(ipDest);   // for clients: server's IP
// for servers binding to any local interface: INADDR_ANY
```
- `htons()` converts an integer port to network byte order
- `inet_addr()` converts a dotted-decimal string to a binary IP address

### TCP Flow — Client vs. Server
```
Server:  socket() → bind() → listen() → accept() → read()/write() → close()
Client:  socket() →                    connect()  → write()/read() → close()
```
- `bind(sockfd, addr, addrlen)` — attaches the socket to a specific local port; server-side
- `listen(sockfd, backlog)` — marks the socket as passive, `backlog` sets the max queued pending connections
- `accept()` — blocks until a client connects, returns a *new* socket descriptor for that specific connection
- `connect()` — client-side; initiates the TCP handshake to the server's address

### UDP Difference
UDP has no `listen()`/`accept()`/`connect()` handshake — after `socket()` and `bind()`, both sides just use `sendto()`/`recvfrom()` directly, since there's no persistent connection state.

- SOA and NS metadata can identify authoritative infrastructure and admins.
- Over-permissive zone transfer behavior leaks host inventory quickly.
- DNS poisoning risks focus on trust in cache and resolver integrity.
- Defenders harden by limiting transfer sources and monitoring anomalous changes.

children.title: DNS Zone Transfer (AXFR) — Exposure Risk
children.label: DNS Zone Transfer
children.summary: An unrestricted AXFR request dumps an entire DNS zone in one query, exposing internal hostnames and network layout that would otherwise take extensive scanning to enumerate.
children.core_idea:
Zone transfers are meant to replicate a DNS zone from a primary server to its secondaries — a legitimate, expected operation between trusted servers. If an authoritative server allows AXFR requests from *any* client, though, an attacker gets the entire zone file in one shot: every subdomain, internal-facing hostname, and inferred network layout.

```
dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com
```

**Mitigation:** explicitly restrict transfers with an `allow-transfer` ACL naming only legitimate secondary servers (e.g. in BIND's zone configuration) — the default should never be "allow from anywhere."

children.title: DHCP — Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
children.label: DHCP
children.summary: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and configuration via a 4-step Discover/Offer/Request/ACK exchange, building on the older BOOTP protocol.
children.core_idea:
### Background — BOOTP
**BOOTP** (Bootstrap Protocol) let diskless workstations be remotely booted on a network by mapping a known MAC address to an IP assignment. Well-known UDP ports: **67** (server), **68** (client) — DHCP inherited these.

### DHCP
Builds on BOOTP to deliver full configuration information to a host and assign **temporary** IP addresses, letting ISPs and network admins maximize use of a limited address pool. **DHCPv6** uses UDP ports **547** (server) / **546** (client).

### 4-Step Operation (DORA)
1. **DHCP Discover** — host broadcasts, looking for any DHCP server
2. **DHCP Offer** — one or more servers reply with an offered IP + configuration
3. **DHCP Request** — host broadcasts, selecting one offer
4. **DHCP ACK** — the selected server confirms and allocates the IP for lease time **T**, along with subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers

### Lease Renewal Timers
- **T₁ = 0.5T** — host attempts to renew directly with the **original** server
- **T₂ = 0.875T** — if no renewal by T₂, host broadcasts to **any** server
- If no reply by **T**, the host must relinquish the address and restart DHCP from scratch

### Real-World Example (`ipconfig /all`)
```
Physical Address  : B0-7B-25-2C-6B-48   ← MAC (OUI = vendor prefix)
DHCP Enabled      : Yes
IPv4 Address      : 10.24.101.130
Subnet Mask       : 255.255.252.0
Default Gateway   : 10.24.103.254
DHCP Server       : 10.10.67.136
Lease Obtained / Expires : [timestamps]
DNS Servers       : [list]
```

### DHCP Starvation (attack)
An attacker rapidly requests every available address in the pool using spoofed MAC addresses, exhausting the DHCP server so legitimate clients can't get an IP — often paired with a rogue DHCP server to then hand out malicious gateway/DNS settings.

children.title: Email Security — Architecture, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, and Spoofing Risks
children.label: Email Security
children.summary: SMTP has no built-in sender authentication; SPF, DKIM, and DMARC layer trust on top of it using DNS-published records.
children.core_idea:
### Email Architecture
- **MTA (Message Transfer Agent)** — routes and delivers mail between servers
- **UA (User Agent)** — the client application a user reads/composes mail with

### Why Email Is Inherently Insecure
- **No host-to-host authentication** — SMTP trusts whatever `MAIL FROM:` claims; the sender's IP could be spoofed and the MTA's recorded "sending IP" can't be fully trusted either
- **Clear-text by default** — messages are stored unencrypted on both the MTA and UA, and legacy UAs send login credentials in clear text
- UAs supporting scripting extensions (e.g. VBA macros in Outlook) expand the attack surface for malicious attachments

### SPF (Sender Policy Framework)
A DNS TXT record listing which mail servers are authorized to send mail for a domain. Receivers check the connecting server's IP against this list.

### DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)
Cryptographically signs outgoing mail with a private key; the public key is published in DNS, letting receivers verify the message wasn't altered in transit and genuinely came from a server holding the domain's private key.

### DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance)
Ties SPF and DKIM together and tells receivers what to do when both fail:
1. Receiver checks the sending IP against the domain's **SPF** record
2. Receiver validates the message signature against the domain's **DKIM** public key
3. Receiver checks **alignment** — does the authenticated SPF/DKIM domain match the visible "From:" domain?
4. If SPF *or* DKIM passes **and** aligns with the visible From domain → DMARC passes
5. If DMARC fails, the receiver acts per the domain's published policy: deliver anyway, quarantine (spam), or reject outright
6. Receivers send the domain owner a daily aggregate report of authentication results across all observed senders — useful for spotting spoofing attempts against your own domain

children.title: Firewalls — Types, Rule Sets & Architecture
children.label: Firewalls
children.summary: Firewalls make default-deny, per-packet decisions — misconfiguration causes more failures than the tech itself.
children.core_idea:
- Firewall = per-packet yes/no forwarding decision against a rule set; **default deny** is the standard posture
- Types: **Dual-Homed Host** (2 NICs, most common, aka pass-through), **Air Gap** (two apps relay traffic between them), **Screening Router** (fast, TCP/IP-layer only, often paired in front of a full firewall)
- Attacked two ways: exploit the firewall's own software, or piggyback malicious traffic over an already-open port (e.g. tunnel through port 80)
- **DMZ** = two firewalls sandwiching exposed "sacrificial" hosts (mail/web/FTP), isolating them from the trusted internal network
- Misconfiguration — not ruleset logic — is the most common real-world firewall vulnerability

children.title: iptables — Stateful Filtering
children.label: iptables
children.summary: Stateful firewalls track connection state (conntrack) so return traffic for an established connection is allowed without opening inbound ports broadly.
children.core_idea:
### Stateful vs. Stateless
A stateless firewall must evaluate every packet against the rule set independently. A stateful firewall tracks connections in a **conntrack table** and can allow return traffic for a connection it has already approved, without a separate inbound rule.

```
iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
iptables -P INPUT DROP
```

### Best Practice Pattern
- **Default-drop** the INPUT chain, then explicitly allow only what's needed
- Allow `ESTABLISHED,RELATED` traffic first so replies to outbound/approved connections aren't re-evaluated from scratch
- Log dropped packets sparingly — verbose logging on a high-drop-rate firewall can itself become a DoS vector (log flooding filling disk/CPU)

commands.explain: Allow return traffic for connections already approved, without opening new inbound ports.

children.title: VLAN Hopping
children.label: VLAN Hopping
children.summary: Double-tagging or switch spoofing tricks a switch into forwarding frames into a VLAN the attacker shouldn't have access to.
children.core_idea:
### Double Tagging
An attacker on the native VLAN sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags. The first switch strips the outer tag (matching the native VLAN) and forwards the frame — the inner tag then gets treated as if it were the original, hopping the frame into a different VLAN than the attacker's actual port.

### Switch Spoofing
If a port is left in dynamic trunking mode, an attacker's host can negotiate a trunk link with the switch (mimicking a legitimate switch), gaining access to all VLANs carried on that trunk.

### Mitigations
- Explicitly configure trunk ports rather than relying on auto-negotiation
- Disable DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) on access ports
- Never use VLAN 1 (the default native VLAN) for user traffic, and ensure native VLAN configuration matches on both ends of a trunk
- Keep the management VLAN separate from user VLANs entirely

children.title: Access Control Models — MAC, DAC & RBAC
children.label: Access Control Models
children.summary: Mandatory Access Control compares security labels/clearances; Role-Based Access Control grants permissions through roles rather than individual users, governed by hierarchy, exclusivity, and cardinality constraints.
children.core_idea:
### Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
Access is controlled centrally by comparing a subject's **security clearance** against an object's **security label/classification** (e.g. Confidential, Secret, Top Secret) — the user cannot change these labels themselves. Common in government/military systems.

### Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
The resource *owner* decides who else gets access (e.g. standard Unix file permissions, ACLs) — more flexible than MAC but weaker for enforcing organization-wide policy since any owner can grant access.

### Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
Access is granted through **roles** rather than directly to individual users — a role bundles a set of permissions, and users are assigned to roles. Roles can be static or dynamic (activated per session).

**Constraints that govern role design:**
- **Hierarchy** — a higher-level role automatically includes all access rights of the roles beneath it
- **Mutual exclusivity** — certain roles cannot be held by the same user simultaneously (e.g. "submit expense" and "approve expense")
- **Cardinality** — limits on role assignment, such as:
  - Maximum number of users who may hold a given role
  - Maximum number of roles a single user may be assigned
- **Prerequisite** — a condition that must already be satisfied before a user can be assigned a given role (e.g. must hold Role A before being eligible for Role B)

RBAC scales far better than assigning permissions per-user directly, and is the dominant model in enterprise identity systems.

children.title: Footprinting & Network Reconnaissance Techniques
children.label: Footprinting & Network Reconnaissance
children.summary: Footprinting profiles a target before attack — DNS, whois, and traceroute are the highest-yield free sources.
children.core_idea:
- Targets three surfaces: **Internet** (domains, IPs, topology), **Intranet** (internal tech, VPNs), **Extranet** (partner-facing access)
- `whois` reveals org/admin contacts and DNS servers; `nslookup`/`dig` resolve hosts and reveal record structure; misconfigured zone transfers expose the entire domain map in one query
- Website mirroring, HTML source comments, and job/social posts from IT staff often leak more than the target intends
- Traceroute (via the TTL trick) reveals path and internal topology; DNS (port 53/UDP) is often open when other UDP ports are filtered, making it a useful probe point

children.title: Adversarial Thinking — Motivations, Goals & Insider Threats
children.label: Adversarial Thinking
children.summary: Adversaries pursue espionage, disruption, or reputation damage — cyber and physical attacks increasingly combine.
children.core_idea:
- Crosscutting goals regardless of motivation: espionage, disruption, reputation damage, resource control, social engineering, intimidation
- Motivations: political, economic, ideological, personal (revenge), technological (IP theft), strategic/military
- **Cyber aids physical**: disabling alarms/cameras before an intrusion, manipulating OT to create physical hazards. **Physical aids cyber**: USB drops, plugging into a network port after building access, supply-chain hardware tampering
- **Insider threats**: intentional (malicious), accidental (leaks via careless use), or intentionally-accidental (social-engineered into "accidentally" leaking data as technical defenses harden)

children.title: ARP & ARP Spoofing — Layer 2 MITM
children.label: ARP & ARP Spoofing
children.summary: ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses with no authentication; forged ARP replies let an attacker poison a victim's cache and sit in the middle of local traffic.
children.core_idea:
### How ARP Works
Address Resolution Protocol maps a known IP address to the MAC address needed to actually deliver a frame on the local segment. A host broadcasts "who has IP X?" and the owner replies with its MAC — the requester caches the mapping.

### ARP Spoofing (Cache Poisoning)
ARP has **no authentication** — any host can claim to own any IP address. An attacker sends forged ("gratuitous") ARP replies claiming to own the gateway's (or another host's) IP, poisoning victims' ARP caches so their traffic routes through the attacker instead — a classic Layer 2 man-in-the-middle.
- Attackers periodically re-send gratuitous ARP to keep the poisoned entry from expiring back to the correct mapping

### Defense
- **Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)** on managed switches, validating ARP packets against a trusted binding table (often built from DHCP snooping)
- **Static ARP entries** for critical infrastructure like default gateways
- Encryption above Layer 2 (TLS, etc.) limits the *value* of a successful MITM even if ARP poisoning succeeds

children.title: ARP Poisoning (MITM)
children.label: ARP Poisoning
children.summary: ARP poisoning forges IP-to-MAC mappings so traffic is redirected through an attacker-controlled host.
children.core_idea:
- Attackers send spoofed ARP replies to overwrite victim cache entries.
- Common goal is man-in-the-middle interception or traffic manipulation.
- Switching does not prevent it because ARP trust is weak by default.
- Frequent spoof updates are typically needed to maintain control.
- Defenses include dynamic ARP inspection, static critical entries, and monitoring.

children.title: MAC Flooding and CAM Table Exhaustion
children.label: MAC Flooding
children.summary: MAC flooding overwhelms a switch CAM table so traffic may be flooded like a hub.
children.core_idea:
- Attack sends many fake source MACs to consume CAM table space.
- Unknown-destination traffic can be flooded, increasing sniffing opportunity.
- Modern switches often mitigate with port-security and rate limits.
- Effectiveness varies by hardware, firmware, and configured protections.
- Even failed attempts are useful detection signals of hostile recon.

children.title: DNS Cache Poisoning Basics
children.label: DNS Cache Poisoning
children.summary: DNS cache poisoning injects false name-to-IP data so users are redirected to attacker-selected destinations.
children.core_idea:
- Attack success relies on resolver trust and cache acceptance behavior.
- Poisoned entries persist until TTL expiry or cache flush.
- Users can be silently redirected even when typing correct domains.
- Hardening includes resolver updates, source-port/randomization, and DNSSEC support.
- Monitor DNS anomalies and sudden answer changes for high-value domains.

children.title: Wireshark Hex Dump — Ethernet/IP/TCP Header Fields
children.label: Wireshark Hex Dump
children.summary: Ethernet is always the first 14 bytes — use IHL and Data Offset nibbles to find where IP and TCP headers end.
children.core_idea:
**Ethernet (14 bytes):** 6B dest MAC, 6B source MAC, 2B EtherType (`0800` = IPv4)

**IPv4 (20+ bytes):** 1B Version/IHL (IHL × 4 = header length in bytes), 2B Total Length, 2B ID (fragment reassembly), 1B TTL, 1B Protocol (`06`=TCP, `11`=UDP, `01`=ICMP), 4B Source IP, 4B Dest IP

**TCP (20+ bytes):** 2B Source Port, 2B Dest Port, 4B Sequence #, 4B Ack #, 1B Data Offset (high nibble → header length), 1B Flags, 2B Window Size

- **Reading order:** Ethernet's first 14 bytes are fixed → IHL nibble gives IP header end → TCP Data Offset nibble gives TCP header end, payload starts after

children.title: Wireshark — Display Filters
children.label: Wireshark
children.summary: Display filters narrow the packet list after capture; the syntax is Wireshark-specific and differs from BPF capture filters.
children.core_idea:
### Display vs. Capture Filters
- **Capture filters** (BPF syntax, e.g. `tcpdump`-style) decide what gets recorded in the first place
- **Display filters** (Wireshark's own syntax) narrow what's shown from an already-captured file — nothing is discarded, so you can always broaden the filter later

### Common Filters
| Filter | Matches |
|---|---|
| `ip.addr == 10.0.0.5` | Traffic to/from an IP |
| `tcp.port == 443` | Traffic on a specific port |
| `http.request` | HTTP request packets only |
| `tls.handshake.type == 1` | TLS ClientHello packets |

Combine filters with `&&` and `||`. Right-click a TCP packet → **Follow → TCP Stream** to reconstruct the full application-layer conversation in one view — invaluable for reading plaintext protocols or reassembling a file transfer.

children.title: ICMP Diagnostics — ping & traceroute
children.label: ICMP Diagnostics
children.summary: ICMP helps map reachability and filtering behavior, not just basic host liveness.
children.core_idea:
- Echo requests/replies support quick host discovery and path checks.
- Type and code responses can indicate unreachable hosts vs blocked traffic.
- Traceroute reveals routing hops and potential choke points.
- ICMP filtering changes recon visibility but does not remove attack surface.
- Use ICMP alongside TCP/UDP probes for accurate network interpretation.

children.title: SSH — Key-Based Authentication & Hardening
children.label: SSH
children.summary: Public-key auth is stronger than passwords; disable password login after deploying keys, and lock down key file permissions.
children.core_idea:
### Setup
- Generate a keypair, copy the public key to the target's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`
- Connect with `ssh -i <keyfile> user@host`

### Required Permissions
SSH refuses to use a key or config that's too permissive:
```
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 <private-key-file>
```

### Hardening
- Once keys are deployed and verified, disable password auth entirely in `sshd_config`: `PasswordAuthentication no`
- **fail2ban** — bans IPs after repeated failed login attempts, mitigating brute force
- **Bastion/jump hosts** — route SSH access to internal machines through a single hardened, monitored entry point rather than exposing every host directly

children.title: Threat Modeling — STRIDE
children.label: Threat Modeling
children.summary: STRIDE sorts threats into six categories, applied per element of a data-flow diagram.
children.core_idea:
- **S**poofing — impersonating a user or system
- **T**ampering — modifying data or code in transit or at rest
- **R**epudiation — denying an action without proof it happened
- **I**nfo disclosure / **D**oS / **E**levation of privilege — exposing data, degrading availability, gaining unauthorized access
- Apply STRIDE per data-flow diagram element, then pair findings with abuse cases and security requirements during design review

children.title: Fault Tree Analysis (FTA)
children.label: Fault Tree Analysis
children.summary: Top-down Boolean model from hazard to basic events — cut sets reveal minimal failure combinations.
children.core_idea:
Top-down Boolean model from hazard to basic events — cut sets reveal minimal failure combinations.

Used in safety-critical systems (IEC 61508). AND/OR gates model component failures. Complements FMEA for systematic hazard analysis.

children.title: FMEA — Failure Mode and Effects Analysis
children.label: FMEA
children.summary: Bottom-up analysis ranking failure modes by Severity × Occurrence × Detection to prioritize design mitigations.
children.core_idea:
Bottom-up analysis ranking failure modes by Severity × Occurrence × Detection to prioritize design mitigations.

Used alongside fault trees in safety-critical systems. Document RPN scores and corrective actions to closure.

children.title: STPA — Systems-Theoretic Hazard Analysis
children.label: STPA
children.summary: STPA models unsafe control actions in complex systems — complements FMEA/FTA for software-intensive designs.
children.core_idea:
STPA models unsafe control actions in complex systems — complements FMEA/FTA for software-intensive designs.

Identify controllers, controlled processes, and feedback loops. Analyze scenarios where control is too early, late, or wrong.

children.title: Secure Coding — Input Validation
children.label: Secure Coding
children.summary: Validate type, length, range, and encoding at every trust boundary — never trust client-side checks alone.
children.core_idea:
- Validate at every trust boundary: type, length, range, and encoding — client-side checks are a UX nicety, not a security control
- **Allowlist over denylist** — define what's acceptable rather than trying to block every bad pattern
- **Canonicalize before validating** — normalize encoding/paths first, or an attacker can smuggle a bad value past the check
- **Separate data from commands** — parameterized queries, not string-concatenated SQL

children.title: Memory Safety — Buffer Overruns in C/C++
children.label: Memory Safety
children.summary: Unchecked bounds on stack/heap buffers enable corruption — use safe APIs, canaries, ASLR, and static analysis.
children.core_idea:
Unchecked bounds on stack/heap buffers enable corruption — use safe APIs, canaries, ASLR, and static analysis.

Prefer `snprintf` over `sprintf`, bounded copies, and languages with memory safety for new components.

children.title: Integer Overflow & Wraparound
children.label: Integer Overflow & Wraparound
children.summary: Fixed-width integer arithmetic can wrap silently, undersizing buffers or bypassing length checks.
children.core_idea:
- Adding/multiplying past a type's max value wraps around instead of erroring — a huge number can silently become tiny (or negative)
- Classic exploit path: attacker-controlled size calculation wraps small, allocation undersizes, later write overflows the buffer
- Defend with safe math libraries, and validate inputs *before* the multiply/add used for buffer sizing — not after
- Enable compiler sanitizers (e.g. UBSan) in CI to catch overflow during testing rather than in production

children.title: Race Conditions & TOCTOU
children.label: Race Conditions & TOCTOU
children.summary: Time-of-check vs time-of-use gaps let attackers swap files or paths between validation and use.
children.core_idea:
Time-of-check vs time-of-use gaps let attackers swap files or paths between validation and use.

Use atomic operations, file descriptors instead of paths, and proper locking. Symlink attacks exploit TOCTOU on temp files.

children.title: Secure Coding — Fail-Secure Error Handling
children.label: Secure Coding
children.summary: On failure, default to deny — close connections, reject requests, and avoid leaking stack traces or internal paths.
children.core_idea:

children.core_idea:

Derive SIL from hazard analysis. Hardware fault tolerance and diagnostic coverage increase with SIL. Trace requirements to tests.

children.title: Software-Based Fault Tolerance on COTS Hardware
children.label: Software
children.summary: Fault tolerance is traditionally handled by specialized hardware; software-based techniques like arithmetic coding let commercial off-the-shelf hardware detect faults instead.
children.core_idea:
### The Problem
Hardware unreliability is a growing concern as systems push commodity hardware harder. Faults are classified by duration:
- **Transient faults** — occur briefly, then disappear (e.g. a cosmic-ray-induced bit flip)
- **Permanent faults** — continuously affect the system once they occur (physical hardware damage)
- **Intermittent faults** — occur briefly but recur periodically, often signaling a developing hardware issue before it becomes permanent

### Traditional Approach vs. Software-Based Alternative
Fault tolerance has traditionally been handled by **specialized, redundant hardware** — and is a hard requirement for safety-critical systems under standards like **IEC 61508**. Specialized fault-tolerant hardware is expensive, though, which motivates research into **software-based fault tolerance** techniques that let commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware achieve comparable fault detection without custom silicon.

**Arithmetic coding** is one such technique — encoding integer calculations in a way that makes corruption from a fault detectable in the result itself, trading some computational overhead for fault-detection capability without needing specialized hardware. The core research tradeoff is exactly that: **detection capability vs. performance overhead** — stronger encoding catches more fault classes but costs more cycles per operation.

children.title: Safety-Critical Hazard Analysis — Case Studies
children.label: Safety
children.summary: Fault Tree Analysis and static code analysis applied to real safety-critical systems (radiosurgery devices, Mars lander software) reveal single-point failure paths before they reach production.
children.core_idea:
Systematic hazard and failure analysis — using **Fault Tree Analysis**, **SFMECA** (Software Failure Mode, Effects, and Criticality Analysis), and formal verification — applied to two illustrative safety-critical domains:

- **Stereotactic radiosurgery devices** — medical systems where a software fault translates directly into patient harm; fault trees here identify **single-point failure paths** (any one component whose failure alone causes the hazard) and derive **minimal cut sets** (the smallest combinations of component failures that together trigger the top-level hazard)
- **Mars lander software** (referencing the well-documented Mars Polar Lander loss) — static code analysis applied to flight software to detect latent defects before launch, since safety-critical embedded software often can't be patched once deployed

**Why this matters for security, not just safety:** the same fault-tree and static-analysis methodology used to find *accidental* failure paths is directly applicable to finding *deliberately exploitable* ones — a single point of failure an engineer worries about for reliability is often the same weak point an attacker would target for disruption.

children.title: Multi-Factor Authentication — Mechanisms & Bypass Patterns
children.label: MFA Mechanisms
children.summary: MFA combines something you know/have/are — but SIM-swap, MFA fatigue, and session-token theft all bypass it.
children.core_idea:
- Factors: **knowledge** (password), **possession** (token/phone), **inherence** (biometric) — true MFA combines factors from different categories
- **MFA fatigue / push bombing** — attacker spams approval requests until the user taps "approve" out of annoyance
- **SIM swapping** — attacker ports the victim's number to intercept SMS-based codes; SMS is the weakest MFA factor
- **Session/token theft** — stealing an already-authenticated session cookie or OAuth token skips MFA entirely, since the user already passed it
- Phishing-resistant options (FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys) block most of the above; SMS OTP should be treated as a fallback, not primary

children.title: Password Policy vs. Passwordless — Tradeoffs
children.label: Password Policy vs Passwordless
children.summary: Complexity rules alone don't stop credential stuffing or phishing — length, MFA, or passwordless do more.
children.core_idea:
- Modern guidance (NIST 800-63B) favors **length over complexity** — long passphrases beat forced special-character rules, which just push users toward predictable patterns
- Traditional password policy doesn't stop **credential stuffing** (reused passwords from other breaches) or phishing — MFA does
- **Passwordless** (FIDO2/WebAuthn, passkeys) removes the shared secret entirely — nothing to phish or stuff
- Tradeoff: passwordless requires device/platform support and a recovery path if the device is lost — not a drop-in replacement everywhere yet

children.title: Password Attack Models (Online vs Offline)
children.label: Password Attack Models
children.summary: Password attacks differ by where guessing occurs: online against a live service or offline against stolen hashes.
children.core_idea:
- Online attacks are throttled by lockout, MFA, and monitoring controls.
- Offline attacks are limited mostly by hash strength and compute power.
- Dictionary/hybrid/brute-force methods trade speed for coverage.
- Long passphrases and modern KDFs materially increase attacker cost.
- Credential reuse turns one compromise into multi-system risk.

children.title: Password Attack Patterns & Mitigations
children.label: Password Attack Patterns &
children.summary: Different password attack patterns call for different defenses — account lockouts stop credential stuffing, but can themselves become a denial-of-service vector.
children.core_idea:
| Attack Pattern | Description | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Popular Password Attack** | Try a small set of very common passwords against many accounts | Block/rate-limit computers making many rapid login attempts |
| **Password Guessing Against a Single User** | Focused brute-force / dictionary attack on one account | User training in password selection; enforce complexity/length |
| **Computer Hijacking** | Attacker gains control of an already-authenticated session | Auto-logout on inactivity |
| **Exploiting User Mistakes** | Social engineering, phishing (LFA-style credential harvesting) | User awareness training |

### Account Lockout Trade-off
Locking an account after N failed attempts stops brute-forcing, but it also hands an attacker a cheap **denial-of-service** lever — deliberately triggering lockouts on legitimate users' accounts. Modern practice favors **rate-limiting and exponential backoff** or **CAPTCHA challenges** over hard lockouts, and phishing-resistant MFA over relying on password strength alone.

children.title: Kerberos Ticket Flow (AS/TGS/TGT)
children.label: Kerberos Ticket Flow
children.summary: Kerberos uses ticket exchanges (AS-REQ/REP and TGS-REQ/REP) to authenticate without repeatedly sending passwords.
children.core_idea:
- Client first obtains a TGT from the Authentication Service path.
- TGT is then used to request service-specific tickets from TGS.
- Mutual trust depends on KDC integrity, clock sync, and key hygiene.
- Ticket theft/relay risks focus on credential material handling, not plaintext passwords.
- Defenses include strong service-account policy and constrained delegation design.

children.title: Identity & Authentication Fundamentals
children.label: Identity & Authentication Fundamentals
children.summary: Authentication has four directions (user↔host↔user) and three factors — infrastructure trust chains are the real failure point.
children.core_idea:
- **Identity** = who/what something is; **Authentication** = validating that claimed identity — the first step of any IAM system
- Four directions: User→Host (login), Host→Host (historically IP-based, weak), User→User (digital signatures), Host→User (TLS certificates)
- Three factors: **know** (password), **have** (token/key card), **are** (biometric) — combine factors from different categories for real MFA
- **Infrastructure failures**: a compromised CA key collapses trust in everything it vouches for; IP-based trust is inherently spoofable — mitigate with Zero Trust (continuous validation, assume breach)
- **Human failures**: phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering — mitigate with phishing-resistant MFA and strict support-staff verification

children.title: AAA Model — Authentication, Authorization, Auditing
children.label: AAA Model
children.summary: Access control has three pillars: verifying identity (authentication), granting permission (authorization), and independently reviewing what happened (auditing).
children.core_idea:
### What Is Access Control?
The "gatekeeper" side of a system — everything that governs what a given identity is allowed to do.

### The Three A's
- **Authentication** — verifying that presented credentials are valid ("are you who you claim to be?")
- **Authorization** — granting a validated entity permission to access a specific resource ("are you allowed to do this?")
- **Audit** — independent review of system records to test whether controls are working, ensure compliance, and detect breaches after the fact

### Subjects & Objects
- **Subject** — the entity requesting access; further classified as **owner**, **group**, or **world** (the classic Unix permission model)
- **Object** — the resource being protected, to which access is being controlled

Authentication and authorization are enforced *in the moment*; auditing is what lets you catch failures of the first two after the fact — all three are necessary for a complete access-control story.

children.title: Why Authentication Really Fails
children.label: Why Authentication Really Fails
children.summary: Authentication almost never fails because the cryptography broke — it fails at the structural boundaries between trust assumptions and human behavior.
children.core_idea:
- **Authentication fails structurally, not cryptographically** — the math behind modern authentication schemes rarely breaks; what breaks are the trust assumptions surrounding it and the humans operating within it
- Most real-world compromises exploit the **boundaries between failure categories** — e.g. a technically sound cryptographic scheme undermined by a social-engineered help-desk reset, or a correct protocol running on top of an over-trusted network identity
- Compromising authentication is rarely the end goal itself — it's the enabler for **lateral movement** and establishing **persistence** inside a target environment
- Resilience requires **layered controls plus active detection** — no single authentication control is sufficient on its own; assume any one layer can fail and design for that
- Given how much downstream access depends on it, **authentication should be treated as a strategic target** in its own right when designing defenses, not as a checkbox

children.title: SSO Basics — SAML vs OIDC
children.label: SSO: SAML vs OIDC
children.summary: SAML is XML-based and enterprise-focused; OIDC is JSON/REST-based and built for modern web/mobile apps.
children.core_idea:
- **SSO** — authenticate once with an Identity Provider (IdP), access multiple Service Providers (SPs) without re-logging in
- **SAML** — XML assertions, browser-redirect flows, dominant in enterprise/legacy SaaS (e.g. Okta → internal apps)
- **OIDC** — built on OAuth 2.0, JSON Web Tokens, REST-friendly — dominant for modern web/mobile and API-driven apps
- Common attack surface: XML Signature Wrapping (SAML), token replay/misconfigured redirect URIs (OIDC) — both hinge on the IdP-SP trust relationship being correctly validated

children.title: Privileged Access Management (PAM)
children.label: PAM
children.summary: Vault, rotate, and monitor privileged credentials so no admin account is a standing, static risk.
children.core_idea:
- Centralizes privileged credentials in a vault rather than letting admins hold static passwords indefinitely
- Enforces **credential rotation** automatically after each checkout/use
- **Session recording** on privileged access — an auditable log of exactly what an admin did with elevated rights
- Pairs naturally with Just-in-Time access — the vault grants time-boxed elevation instead of standing admin rights

children.title: Just-in-Time (JIT) Access
children.label: JIT Access
children.summary: Grant elevated access only for the duration needed, then automatically revoke it.
children.core_idea:
- Standing admin/root access is a persistent target — JIT collapses that window to only when work is actually happening
- Typical flow: request → approval (manual or policy-based) → time-boxed grant → automatic revocation
- Reduces the value of a compromised credential — even a stolen account has no elevated rights outside an approved window
- Common in cloud IAM (temporary elevated roles) and PAM tooling (checkout-based privileged sessions)

children.label: Web Security

children.title: Web Fundamentals — URLs, CGI & Apache Access Control
children.label: Web Fundamentals
children.summary: HTTP is stateless (cookies bolt on state); unsanitized CGI input is a classic shell-injection path.
children.core_idea:
- Request flow: browser → web server → (if dynamic) app server → database; HTTP itself is a stateless file-transport protocol
- URL structure: `scheme://[user:password]@hostname:[port]/path` — default ports 80 (HTTP) / 443 (HTTPS)
- Key `httpd.conf` directives: `DocumentRoot`, `UserDir`, `AccessFileName` (usually `.htaccess`), `Alias`/`ScriptAlias`, `IndexIgnore`
- CGI lets server-side code process user input — classic exploit: `nobody; cat /etc/passwd` — an unescaped `;` becomes a shell command separator
- Never store password/group files inside the document tree — anything in there is readable over plain HTTP

children.title: Web Server & Application Attack Categories
children.label: Web Server & Application
children.summary: Web compromise usually combines software flaws, weak config, and over-privileged runtime context.
children.core_idea:
- Patch lag and exposed defaults create recurring exploit windows.
- Verbose errors and banners leak stack details useful for targeting.
- Unsafe CGI/SSI and weak file permissions widen execution paths.
- Running web services with excessive privileges magnifies impact.
- Hardening should pair config baselines with regular verification scans.

children.title: OWASP Top 10 — Priority Web Risks
children.label: OWASP Top 10
children.summary: Broken access control and injection consistently rank highest — map findings to Top 10 for stakeholder communication.
children.core_idea: Use the OWASP Top 10 as a **coverage checklist** during assessments and a common vocabulary for communicating findings to stakeholders — not as an exhaustive risk list on its own. For depth beyond the Top 10's headline categories, pair it with the **OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard)**, which breaks each category into specific, testable requirements.

children.title: Application & Freeware Firewalls
children.label: Application & Freeware Firewalls
children.summary: Application firewalls are built into the software they protect (WAFs being the most common); freeware firewalls range from router-embedded to OS-level personal firewalls.
children.core_idea:
### Application Firewalls
Integrated directly into an application rather than sitting in front of it as a separate device. The most common case is the **Web Application Firewall (WAF)** — inspects HTTP traffic at the application layer for attack patterns (SQLi, XSS payloads, etc.) that a network-layer firewall can't see.

### Freeware / Consumer Firewalls
| Firewall | Where It Runs |
|---|---|
| Built-in router firewall | Most home access/routers |
| **pfSense** / **OPNsense** | Dedicated open-source firewall distributions |
| **ZoneAlarm** and similar | Personal, OS-level firewall software |

Most desktop/mobile OSes also ship a built-in personal firewall as a baseline — freeware/open-source options generally add more granular rule control and logging than the OS default.

children.title: SQL Injection — UNION-Based
children.label: SQL Injection
children.summary: SQL injection happens when untrusted input changes query intent and reaches the database interpreter.
children.core_idea:
- Common forms include UNION-based, tautology, blind, and error-based injection.
- Impact ranges from auth bypass to data theft and destructive writes.
- Parameterized queries and strict input validation are primary defenses.
- Least-privileged DB accounts reduce blast radius when bugs exist.
- Detailed DB error messages help attackers and should be suppressed.

children.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
children.label: Cross
children.summary: XSS executes attacker-controlled script in a trusted browser context, often to steal session state.
children.core_idea:
- Reflected XSS comes from immediate request/response echo paths.
- Stored XSS persists in backend data and affects many users.
- Payloads often target cookies, tokens, and DOM-based trust assumptions.
- Defenses include output encoding, CSP, and safe template patterns.
- Session theft risk rises when cookies are not hardened (HttpOnly/SameSite/Secure).

children.title: Client-Side Web Attack Techniques
children.label: Client
children.summary: Browser-side attacks bypass server defenses entirely — MitB, session hijacking, and clickjacking are highest-impact.
children.core_idea:
| Attack | How |
|---|---|
| Man-in-the-Browser | Malware silently alters transactions (e.g. bank transfers) in the browser itself |
| Session Hijacking | Steals a session cookie to impersonate the logged-in user |
| Clickjacking | Invisible iframe redirects a click; defend with CSP `frame-ancestors` / `X-Frame-Options` |
| SSL Stripping | Downgrades HTTPS to HTTP to intercept traffic in transit |
| DNS Spoofing | Forged DNS responses redirect the victim to a malicious site |
| Watering Hole | Compromises a site the target group visits regularly |
| Malvertising | Malicious code hidden inside ad content |
| Cryptojacking | Mining script runs in the visitor's browser, stealing CPU |
| Browser Fingerprinting | Tracks via OS/browser/fonts/screen combo — no cookies needed |
| LFI / RFI | Server includes an attacker-chosen local or remote file |
| WebRTC Leak | Reveals the real IP address even behind a VPN |

children.title: Cookie Poisoning and Session Hijacking
children.label: Cookie Session Hijack
children.summary: Session compromise occurs when attackers steal or tamper with cookies used for authentication state.
children.core_idea:
- Stolen session cookies can bypass credential prompts and impersonate users.
- Client-side editable cookie values should never control privilege decisions.
- Harden with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, and short session lifetimes.
- Rotate session identifiers after login and sensitive privilege changes.
- Monitor impossible-travel and concurrent-session anomalies.

children.title: CSRF — Token & SameSite Defenses
children.label: CSRF
children.summary: CSRF succeeds when browsers auto-send trusted state without verifying user intent.
children.core_idea:
- Use per-request anti-CSRF tokens validated server-side.
- Enforce SameSite and origin/referrer checks for state-changing actions.
- Avoid GET for sensitive operations and require explicit re-auth for critical actions.
- Session and cookie hygiene directly affects CSRF impact.
- Test CSRF controls with realistic multi-step authenticated flows.

children.title: Web Hardening Baseline (Apache/IIS)
children.label: Web Hardening Baseline
children.summary: Web hardening starts by minimizing exposed functionality and continuously validating secure configuration.
children.core_idea:
- Patch web server, runtime, and modules on a tested but timely cadence.
- Disable unused services, handlers, sample apps, and default accounts.
- Suppress verbose errors and banners that leak stack metadata.
- Run services with least privilege and strict file permission boundaries.
- Validate baseline regularly with targeted web vulnerability scans.

children.summary: Grant minimum actions/resources required.

children.core_idea:
Security groups are stateful instance-level firewalls; NACLs are stateless subnet-level filters evaluated in order.
