children.title: EC2 — Instance Hardening Baseline
children.label: EC2
children.summary: Disable unnecessary services, patch AMIs, use IMDSv2, restrict SSH to bastion, and attach instance profiles instead of static keys.
children.core_idea:
Disable unnecessary services, patch AMIs, use IMDSv2, restrict SSH to bastion, and attach instance profiles instead of static keys.

Use Systems Manager Session Manager for shell access without open port 22. Enable EBS encryption by default. Tag instances for ownership and environment.

children.title: AWS Lambda — Least-Privilege Execution Roles
children.label: AWS Lambda
children.summary: Each function needs its own IAM role with only required actions on specific resource ARNs — avoid wildcard policies.
children.core_idea:
Each function needs its own IAM role with only required actions on specific resource ARNs — avoid wildcard policies.

Watch for overly broad `s3:*` or `dynamodb:*`. VPC-attached Lambdas need extra ENI permissions. Scan env vars for leaked keys.

children.title: S3 — Public Bucket Misconfiguration
children.label: S3
children.summary: Block Public Access at the account level; audit for `Principal: *` in ACLs and bucket policies.
children.core_idea:
- Enable **S3 Block Public Access** at the account level as a baseline — don't rely on per-bucket settings alone
- Audit ACLs and bucket policies for `"Principal": "*"`, which grants access to anyone on the internet
- One of the most common real-world cloud breach vectors — misconfiguration, not a code exploit
- Use **Macie** (sensitive data discovery) and **Config rules** for continuous detection; encrypt data at rest with **KMS**

children.title: Secrets Management — AWS Secrets Manager
children.label: Secrets Management
children.summary: Never embed secrets in code or AMIs; use Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store with rotation and IAM-scoped access.
children.core_idea:
Never embed secrets in code or AMIs; use Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store with rotation and IAM-scoped access.

Audit GetSecretValue in CloudTrail. Prefer task roles over environment variables in ECS/Lambda where possible.

children.title: Data Loss — "Data Is Like Water"
children.label: Data Loss
children.summary: Data, like water, is hard to contain once it leaves its original boundary — and unlike water, it can be copied infinitely, making containment even harder.
children.core_idea:
A useful mental model for data loss prevention conversations:
- Data makes up the bulk of what an organization actually *is*, the way water makes up most of the earth's surface
- Data is **hard to hold onto once it leaves its container** — once it's copied to an email, a USB drive, or a personal device, pulling it back is often impossible
- People are often **willing to share data when asked**, especially by someone who sounds authoritative or trusted — the same dynamic that makes social engineering effective
- The key place the analogy breaks down: **data can be copied** infinitely without depleting the original, unlike water — meaning a single leak doesn't just relocate the asset, it multiplies it

children.title: Container Security — Image Scanning
children.label: Container Security
children.summary: Scan images in CI and registry (ECR, Trivy) for CVEs before deploy; pin digests, not mutable tags.
children.core_idea:
Scan images in CI and registry (ECR, Trivy) for CVEs before deploy; pin digests, not mutable tags.

Run as non-root, read-only root filesystem, drop capabilities. Use admission controllers in Kubernetes to block critical CVEs.

children.title: Kubernetes — RBAC Basics
children.label: Kubernetes
children.summary: Roles bind verbs to resources; RoleBindings attach subjects. ClusterRoles span namespaces — avoid cluster-admin for apps.
children.core_idea:
Roles bind verbs to resources; RoleBindings attach subjects. ClusterRoles span namespaces — avoid cluster-admin for apps.

Audit with `kubectl auth can-i`. Use namespaces for tenancy. Service accounts should have minimal permissions.

children.title: CMS (Content Management Systems) — Security Model
children.label: CMS
children.summary: CMS platforms like WordPress/Drupal run as an application layer with their own auth, so their plugin ecosystem — not the underlying OS — is usually the real attack surface.
children.core_idea:
- Most servers run a **CMS** (WordPress, Drupal, etc.) to power websites, common in cloud-hosted environments where users never need direct access to the underlying server OS
- The CMS runs as an application on top of the server and maintains its **own authentication system**, separate from OS-level accounts
- **Third-party plugins** extend functionality but are also the most common source of vulnerabilities — a plugin ecosystem effectively multiplies the attack surface beyond what the core CMS codebase alone would have

children.title: CloudTrail — API Audit Logging
children.label: CloudTrail
children.summary: CloudTrail records API/management events — enable an org-wide trail with log file validation.
children.core_idea:
- Records every management-plane API call (who did what, when, from where) across your AWS account
- Enable an **organization trail** (covers all accounts) rather than per-account trails you might forget
- Turn on **log file validation** to detect tampering, and protect the destination S3 bucket with a lifecycle/retention policy
- Pair with **CloudWatch alarms** on root login, IAM policy changes, and security group opens — logging without alerting just accumulates unread data

children.title: CloudWatch — Security Event Alarms
children.label: CloudWatch
children.summary: Metric filters on CloudTrail log groups can alarm on root login, IAM policy changes, and failed console logins.
children.core_idea:
Metric filters on CloudTrail log groups can alarm on root login, IAM policy changes, and failed console logins.

Route alarms to SNS → ticketing. Tune thresholds to avoid alert fatigue. Combine with GuardDuty findings for correlation.

children.title: AWS GuardDuty — Threat Detection
children.label: AWS GuardDuty
children.summary: GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS for malicious activity — no agents required.
children.core_idea:
GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS for malicious activity — no agents required.

Enable in all regions. Suppress known benign findings after review. Export to Security Hub for centralized posture.

children.title: Chain of Custody
children.label: Chain of Custody
children.summary: Every handoff of evidence must be documented with who, when, and why — any undocumented gap can jeopardize admissibility in court.
children.core_idea:
### Core Requirement
Document **who** handled a piece of evidence, **when**, and **why**, at every single transfer — from initial acquisition through to presentation in court. Any undocumented break in that chain gives opposing counsel grounds to challenge the evidence's integrity, regardless of how technically sound the underlying analysis was.

### Practical Controls
- **Write blockers** — hardware devices that physically prevent any write operation to the source disk during acquisition, guaranteeing the original media is never modified
- **Cryptographic hashing on acquisition** (SHA-256) — hash the source immediately upon imaging, and re-verify that hash at every subsequent step to prove the data hasn't changed
- **Work on copies, never the master** — store the original acquired image read-only, and perform all analysis on a working copy, so the master remains available as an unimpeachable reference if anything is ever questioned

commands.explain: Hash a disk image immediately after acquisition to establish an integrity baseline.
Re-verify the image against its original hash at any later step in the chain.

children.title: Legal Issues in Cybersecurity — Criminal vs. Civil Law
children.label: Legal Issues in Cybersecurity
children.summary: Criminal cybercrime cases need proof beyond a reasonable doubt; civil cases need only a preponderance of evidence — and cross-border jurisdiction complicates both.
children.core_idea:
### Criminal vs. Civil Law
| | Criminal Law | Civil Law |
|---|---|---|
| **Standard of proof** | Beyond a reasonable doubt | Preponderance of evidence (>50%) |
| **Typical use** | Prosecuting cybercrime directly | IP disputes, defamation, harassment |
| **Challenge** | Juries often struggle with technical detail, making prosecution harder despite newer, clearer statutes | Setting damages for a purely digital harm is difficult |

### Key Legal Challenges
- **Unauthorized access laws** are often ambiguously worded and hard to prosecute cleanly
- **Damages in civil cases** are hard to quantify when the harm is data exposure or downtime rather than a physical loss
- Software vendors have historically avoided liability for security bugs in their products, though this is shifting as breach severity increases
- **International jurisdiction** is one of the biggest practical obstacles — laws differ sharply across borders, and attribution (proving *who* did it, in a court-admissible way) is difficult even when the technical evidence is clear

### Types of Protected Information
Copyright, unauthorized-access statutes, theft laws, and domain-specific regulation (e.g. **HIPAA** for medical information) each carry their own legal framework and evidentiary standard — an investigator needs to know which regime applies before evidence collection even begins.

children.title: Forensic Tool Validation & the "Black Box" Defense
children.label: Forensic Tool Validation &
children.summary: Validate forensic tools against a known dataset (Daubert standard) — don't assume any tool is infallible.
children.core_idea:
- **Daubert standard** requires forensic evidence come from methods with a known, tested error rate — measure your tool, don't just trust its brand
- Case study (Autopsy v4.22.1): 100% accurate on allocated files, ~80% on deliberately deleted files (filesystem behavior, not a tool flaw), plus a timezone display bug
- NTFS deletion just flags the MFT entry and frees disk space — metadata can still say "here" after the content is already overwritten
- Open-source ≠ less reliable: Autopsy's failures were filesystem limits any tool would hit, not open-source-specific bugs
- Lightweight validation protocol: keep a golden known-content image, re-test each tool version on a schedule, verify hashes match, log any behavior deviation

children.title: Disk Imaging with dd / dc3dd
children.label: Disk Imaging with dd
children.summary: A forensically sound disk image is a verified bit-for-bit copy, acquired through a hardware write blocker, with every detail of the acquisition logged.
children.core_idea:
### Acquisition
```
dc3dd if=/dev/sdX of=evidence.img hash=sha256 log=acquisition.log
```
`dc3dd` (a forensics-oriented fork of `dd`) adds built-in hashing and logging that plain `dd` lacks — both important for chain-of-custody documentation.

### Requirements for a Sound Acquisition
- **Hardware write blocker** — always, no exceptions; a purely software-based write-blocking approach is a much weaker guarantee under scrutiny
- **Verify with a hash** before any analysis begins — confirm the image matches the source, and re-verify against that same hash at every later step
- **Record serial numbers and tool versions** in the case notes — down to the exact drive serial and imaging software version, since this level of detail is exactly what a validation challenge (see the "Black Box" defense) will probe first

commands.explain: Create a forensic disk image with built-in hashing and an acquisition log.
Plain dd bit-for-bit copy with progress reporting — hash separately before/after if using this instead of dc3dd.

children.title: Memory Forensics — Volatility Basics
children.label: Memory Forensics
children.summary: RAM captures reveal running processes, live network connections, and in-memory malware that never touches disk — but only if the analysis profile matches the source kernel.
children.core_idea:
### Why Memory Matters
A disk image alone misses anything that only ever existed in memory — active network connections, decrypted keys held in process memory, and **fileless malware** that runs entirely in RAM without ever writing itself to disk.

### Key Requirement
The analysis **profile must match the source system's kernel** exactly — Volatility (and similar tools) rely on kernel-specific memory-structure offsets to interpret a raw memory dump correctly; a mismatched profile produces garbage or missed artifacts, not just a warning.

### What to Hunt For
- **Injected code** — legitimate processes with foreign code mapped into their address space
- **Process hollowing** — a legitimate process is emptied out and replaced with malicious code while keeping the original process's name/PID, evading naive process-listing checks
- **Command lines in `_EPROCESS`** — the Windows kernel process structure retains the original invocation command line, often revealing exactly how a malicious process was launched even after the fact

children.title: IDS Functional Components — Sources, Analysis & Response
children.label: IDS Functional Components
children.summary: Every IDS answers three questions: where is it watching (information sources), how does it decide something's wrong (analysis method), and what happens next (response).
children.core_idea:
### 1. Information Sources — Where Is It Monitoring?
Host, network, or application layer — each sees a different slice of activity (see the architecture comparison below).

### 2. Analysis — Is This an Intrusion?
| Method | How It Works |
|---|---|
| **Misuse detection** (signature-based) | Matches traffic against known attack patterns |
| **Virus detection** | Matches against known malware signatures specifically |
| **Anomaly detection** | Flags behavior that deviates from an established normal-use baseline |

### 3. Response — What Happens After Detection?
- **Active response** — an automated action: reconfiguring a firewall on the fly, blocking a scanning IP, or (rarely, and legally fraught) attacking back
- **Passive response** — alarms, notifications, logs, and reports — no automated intervention

### IDS Management Architectures
| Architecture | Description | Drawback |
|---|---|---|
| **Centralized** | One console controls N monitors | Doesn't scale well |
| **Partially Distributed** | N consoles, M monitors, one main console — local processing, major alerts escalate up | Balances scale vs. visibility |
| **Distributed** | Consoles operate independently, no cross-console interaction | Can't recognize a coordinated, system-wide attack from any single console's view |

Also consider placement: **outside** the perimeter (sees raw internet-facing attack attempts) vs. **inside** (sees what actually made it through).

### Timing
- **Interval-based** — periodic polling of collection points; typical for host-based IDS
- **Real-time** — continuous; typical for network-based IDS, where traffic can't be "caught up on" later

children.title: IDS Deployment Types — Network, Host & Application-Based
children.label: IDS Deployment Types
children.summary: Network IDS sees broad traffic but can't inspect encrypted payloads; host IDS sees deep detail but only on one machine and is vulnerable to being disabled by whoever owns that machine.
children.core_idea:
### Network-Based IDS
Essentially a **packet sniffer** deployed at a strategic network point.

**Advantages:** few monitors needed (sometimes just one), minimal network impact, typically runs on a separate/out-of-band management network, and is inherently secure since the sensor itself usually runs no other services.

**Disadvantages:** traffic volume can overwhelm it; some attacks only become visible across *multiple* packets; packets arrive at line speed, making it hard to keep up; **switched networks** don't naturally share traffic to a single point; **encrypted traffic** can't be inspected at all; it can't confirm whether an observed attack actually *succeeded*; and **fragmentation-based evasion** works well against it.

**Switched-network workaround:** a hub/tap inserted between switches, a **mirrored/SPAN port** configured on the switch, or a **dual-port IDS** — traffic between hosts on different switches can also be captured via a tap on the inter-switch uplink.

### Host-Based IDS
Runs directly on the monitored host, drawing from system logs and OS-level activity.

**Advantages:** sees host-level detail invisible to the network, works fine against **encrypted** traffic (it inspects post-decryption), unaffected by switching, and can detect **Trojans** that a network sensor would never see.

**Disadvantages:** management overhead scales with host count; since the **user owns the machine**, they can disable the IDS entirely; it's blind to **network-wide scanning** patterns; vulnerable to local DoS against the host itself; can consume significant CPU processing its own data volume; and its console traffic travels **in-band**, sharing fate with the very network it's trying to protect.

### Application-Based IDS
Typically deployed on web servers, watching **user interaction** at the application layer, and — like host-based IDS — works fine against encrypted traffic.

**Disadvantages:** runs at user privilege level, making it inherently less secure than something running with elevated/kernel access.

children.title: IDS Analysis Methods — Signature vs. Anomaly Detection
children.label: IDS Analysis Methods
children.summary: IDS programs combine signature and anomaly logic; strength comes from layering both approaches.
children.core_idea:
- Signature detection is precise for known threats but misses novel payloads.
- Anomaly detection catches behavior drift but needs careful baselining.
- Noisy scans and floods test IDS thresholds and analyst workflow.
- Context (asset criticality + protocol role) improves triage quality.
- Best practice: correlate IDS events with logs, endpoint, and identity telemetry.

children.title: Snort — Signature-Based IDS Rules
children.label: Snort
children.summary: Snort signatures convert known attack patterns into actionable network detections.
children.core_idea:
- Rules match protocol, direction, content, and context in packet streams.
- Tune signatures to reduce false positives in your environment.
- Use SQLi/XSS-focused rules on web-facing segments for early warning.
- Pair alerting with response playbooks to avoid alert-only operations.
- Continuously update signatures as attack payloads evolve.

commands.explain: Run Snort in live IDS mode against a specific interface using a rule config.

children.title: Sigma — Portable Detection Rules
children.label: Sigma
children.summary: Sigma's YAML format converts to Splunk, Elastic, and Sentinel queries, letting detection logic be shared across SIEM platforms instead of rewritten per tool.
children.core_idea:
Write detection logic once in Sigma's generic YAML format, then convert it to the query syntax of whichever SIEM you actually run (Splunk SPL, Elastic KQL/EQL, Microsoft Sentinel, etc.) — avoids maintaining parallel, drifting rule sets across platforms.

- Map each rule to its corresponding **MITRE ATT&CK** technique tags for coverage tracking
- Version rules with an explicit `status` field (experimental/test/stable) so detection maturity is visible at a glance
- Test every rule against representative log samples before promoting it to production — a rule that's never fired against real data is an unverified assumption, not a working detection

children.title: Tripwire File Integrity Monitoring
children.label: Tripwire FIM
children.summary: File integrity monitoring detects unauthorized change by comparing trusted baselines against current state.
children.core_idea:
- Baselines include critical binaries, configs, and security-sensitive paths.
- Hash/attribute drift signals potential tampering or persistence activity.
- Alert quality depends on tuned scope and approved-change workflows.
- FIM is high-value after suspected malware or privilege escalation events.
- Pair with endpoint and log telemetry for confident triage.

children.title: SIEM — Correlation Use Cases
children.label: SIEM
children.summary: SIEM value comes from correlating events across sources — a single failed login is noise, but failed-then-success-from-a-new-geo is a signal.
children.core_idea:
### High-Value Correlation Patterns
- **Auth failures followed by success from a new geography** — suggests a successful brute-force or credential-stuffing attempt rather than a legitimate user simply mistyping a password
- **Impossible travel** — logins from geographically distant locations within a timeframe no real user could physically travel
- **Privilege escalation sequences** — a chain of individually-unremarkable actions that together indicate an account gaining access it shouldn't have

### Operational Practices
- **Normalize all timestamps to UTC** before correlation — timezone mismatches between log sources are a common source of both false negatives and false alibi-breaking errors (see the digital forensics domain's Autopsy case study for a concrete example of this exact failure mode)
- **Define use cases before ingesting data**, not after — undirected log collection without a correlation goal in mind produces volume without insight
- **Measure MTTD/MTTR** (Mean Time to Detect / Mean Time to Respond) per rule to know which detections are actually earning their operational cost

### Authentication-Specific Indicators Worth Correlating
A breached authentication system can go entirely undetected without dedicated monitoring — detection completes the defense loop that prevention alone cannot close:
- Impossible travel (login from two distant locations in a short window)
- Abnormal Kerberos Ticket Granting Service (TGS) request patterns
- Excessive or unusual MFA prompts (a signal of MFA-fatigue attacks)
- Ticket lifetime anomalies — tickets used well outside their expected validity window

children.title: Log Source Prioritization — What to Alert On First
children.label: Log Source Priority
children.summary: Prioritize identity, endpoint, and perimeter logs first — they carry the highest signal-to-noise for real attacks.
children.core_idea:
- Highest priority: authentication logs (identity provider, VPN), EDR/endpoint telemetry, and perimeter/firewall logs — these catch initial access and lateral movement first
- DNS logs are underrated — most malware and C2 traffic touches DNS at some point, even when it evades other controls
- Don't try to alert on everything at once — start with the log sources tied to your highest-value assets, then expand
- Review and re-tune source priority periodically — what mattered most last year isn't necessarily what matters most now

children.title: UNIX Logging Fundamentals — last/utmp/wtmp, syslog & Rootkit Targets
children.label: UNIX Logging Fundamentals
children.summary: Core UNIX logs (last/utmp/wtmp/syslog) are attacker-modifiable — pair with Tripwire/Swatch for real detection.
children.core_idea:
- `last`/`utmp`/`wtmp` track logins but are trivially editable by root — none are tamper-evident on their own
- `syslogd` collects from `/dev/log` (local), `/dev/klog` (kernel), UDP 514 (remote); `syslog.conf` maps facility+severity → destination
- Facilities: kern, user, mail, auth, cron, local0–8. Severities (high→low): emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug
- `sulog` and `ps` output are classic first rootkit targets — don't trust either on a host you suspect is compromised
- **Tripwire** hashes binaries to catch tampering (run via cron); **Swatch** does real-time log pattern alerting

commands.explain: syslog.conf line: forward auth-facility notices to a remote log server.

children.title: tcpdump CLI Packet Analysis
children.label: tcpdump Basics
children.summary: tcpdump captures packet data from interfaces using precise command-line filters for rapid network triage.
children.core_idea:
- Target specific interfaces and protocols to reduce noise quickly.
- Use capture filters up front to limit volume and preserve relevance.
- Write captures for later deep analysis in tools like Wireshark.
- Great for validating alerts, tracing flows, and confirming exposure.
- Command-line speed makes it useful in incident response under time pressure.

children.title: EDR vs Traditional AV
children.label: EDR vs AV
children.summary: AV blocks known-bad files by signature; EDR watches behavior across the whole endpoint and gives responders a timeline.
children.core_idea:
- **Traditional AV** — signature/hash-based, blocks known-bad files, mostly silent about anything novel or fileless
- **EDR** — behavioral monitoring across process, network, and file activity; flags *suspicious behavior*, not just known-bad signatures
- EDR gives responders a forensic timeline (what ran, what it touched, what it connected to) — AV typically just says "blocked" or "not blocked"
- Most modern endpoint stacks run both — AV/NGAV for baseline blocking, EDR for detection, investigation, and response on what gets through

children.title: SOC Tiering — T1/T2/T3 Roles & Escalation
children.label: SOC Tiering
children.summary: T1 triages and escalates, T2 investigates deeply, T3 hunts and builds detections — escalation criteria should be explicit.
children.core_idea:
- **Tier 1** — initial alert triage: confirm real vs. false positive, gather basic context, escalate anything confirmed or ambiguous
- **Tier 2** — deeper investigation: correlates across sources, scopes the incident, coordinates containment
- **Tier 3** — threat hunting, detection engineering, and the hardest/most novel incidents; often mentors T1/T2
- Clear, written escalation criteria (not "escalate if it feels bad") keeps triage consistent across shifts and analysts

children.title: Alert Triage — Severity × Asset Criticality
children.label: Alert Triage Prioritization
children.summary: Prioritize by severity multiplied by asset criticality, not alert volume or raw CVSS score alone.
children.core_idea:
- Priority = **severity of the alert** × **criticality of the asset it touches** — a medium alert on a domain controller often outranks a high alert on a test box
- Enrich before triaging: known-bad IOC match, asset owner, business context — raw alert text alone is rarely enough to decide
- Track and periodically review false-positive rate per alert rule — a noisy rule that's always wrong erodes analyst trust and slows response to real alerts
- Document triage decisions (not just outcomes) — the reasoning is what improves the next analyst's judgment, not just the ticket closure

children.title: Honeypots, HoneyNets & Padded Cells
children.label: Honeypots, HoneyNets & Padded
children.summary: Deception systems generate high-signal alerts and controlled intel on attacker behavior.
children.core_idea:
- Honeypots are decoy assets designed to attract unauthorized interaction.
- Honeynets expand deception into realistic multi-host environments.
- Padded-cell concepts isolate attackers inside monitored containment zones.
- Any interaction with deception assets is usually high-confidence suspicious activity.
- Use strict segmentation so deception systems do not increase blast radius.

children.title: Incident Response Lifecycle (NIST)
children.label: Incident Response Lifecycle
children.summary: Prepare → Detect/Analyze → Contain → Eradicate → Recover → Lessons Learned. Document decisions in real time.
children.core_idea:
Prepare → Detect/Analyze → Contain → Eradicate → Recover → Lessons Learned. Document decisions in real time.

Containment may be network isolation, account disable, or WAF block. Preserve forensic images before eradication on critical incidents.

children.title: IR — Containment Strategies
children.label: IR
children.summary: Contain fast enough to stop spread, slow enough to preserve evidence and business continuity.
children.core_idea:
- Core tension: contain **too fast** and you tip off the attacker or lose forensic evidence; contain **too slow** and the incident spreads
- **Short-term containment** — isolate the affected host/segment immediately (network isolation, disable account) to stop active spread
- **Long-term containment** — rebuild on clean infrastructure while the root cause is fully understood, rather than just patching in place
- Get legal/comms approval *before* any external notification — containment decisions can have regulatory and PR consequences
- Document every containment action taken and why, in real time — this becomes part of the incident timeline

children.title: IR Eradication — Malware Removal & Patch Validation
children.label: IR Eradication
children.summary: Remove persistence, rotate compromised credentials, and validate patches before reconnection — partial eradication guarantees recurrence.
children.core_idea:
Remove persistence, rotate compromised credentials, and validate patches before reconnection — partial eradication guarantees recurrence.

Hunt for secondary backdoors. Rebuild gold images when rootkits suspected. Verify IOCs absent in follow-up scans.

children.title: IR Recovery — Service Restoration & Enhanced Monitoring
children.label: IR Recovery
children.summary: Restore from clean backups, validate integrity, and increase logging on affected segments during the watch period.
children.core_idea:
Restore from clean backups, validate integrity, and increase logging on affected segments during the watch period.

Define success criteria with business owners. Gradual return beats big-bang if dependencies are uncertain.

children.title: IR Preparation — Runbooks & Contact Lists
children.label: IR Preparation
children.summary: Maintain current runbooks, escalation trees, and vendor contacts before an incident — speed under pressure depends on prep.
children.core_idea:
Maintain current runbooks, escalation trees, and vendor contacts before an incident — speed under pressure depends on prep.

Include forensic tooling access, legal counsel, and comms templates. Test runbooks in tabletops quarterly.

children.title: IR Tabletop Exercises
children.label: IR Tabletop Exercises
children.summary: Facilitated walkthroughs of ransomware/breach/insider scenarios expose gaps in roles and runbooks before a real incident does.
children.core_idea:
- Run scripted scenarios (ransomware, data breach, insider threat) with the actual IR team walking through their real roles
- Inject complications mid-exercise (legal hold, media inquiry, exec unavailable) to test decision-making under pressure, not just the runbook steps
- Capture every gap found as an action item with a named owner and due date — an exercise with no follow-up just repeats the same gaps next time
- Run at least annually, and after any major team or infrastructure change — a stale runbook is worse than a known gap

children.title: IR Detection & Alert Triage
children.label: IR Detection & Alert
children.summary: Prioritize alerts by asset criticality, confidence, and blast radius — not every SIEM rule equals an incident.
children.core_idea:
Prioritize alerts by asset criticality, confidence, and blast radius — not every SIEM rule equals an incident.

Define severity matrix (P1–P4). Enrich with threat intel and asset context. Document false-positive feedback to detection engineering.

children.title: Threat Hunting During Active IR
children.label: Threat Hunting During Active
children.summary: Hypothesis-driven searches across endpoints and logs to find compromise beyond the original alert.
children.core_idea:
- Start from a hypothesis (e.g. "if this technique was used, what else would it touch?"), not a blind log scroll
- Map hunts to specific **MITRE ATT&CK** techniques already observed, to find related activity from the same actor
- Use stacked aggregations in the SIEM (e.g. rare parent-child process pairs) to surface outliers a single alert would miss
- Document negative findings too — "hunted for X, found nothing" narrows scope for the next analyst and proves coverage

children.title: IR Evidence Preservation — Chain of Custody
children.label: IR Evidence Preservation
children.summary: Evidence handling must preserve integrity and timeline fidelity from collection to handoff.
children.core_idea:
- Capture volatile data first when business and legal constraints allow.
- Maintain chain-of-custody records for every transfer and access.
- Use cryptographic hashes to verify evidence integrity over time.
- Preservation decisions should be tied to investigation objectives and scope.
- Separate containment actions from evidence tampering risk.

children.title: Post-Incident Reporting
children.label: Post
children.summary: Post-incident reports should prioritize actionable risk reduction over narrative detail.
children.core_idea:
- Lead with executive-impact summary and affected business scope.
- Document findings ordered by risk and exploitability.
- Attach supporting evidence, timelines, and confidence level for each claim.
- Map each finding to remediation owner and verification step.
- Track unresolved residual risk and follow-up review dates.

children.title: IR Root Cause Analysis — 5 Whys
children.label: IR Root Cause Analysis
children.summary: Iterative why questioning finds systemic causes beyond the immediate vulnerability — fix processes, not just patches.
children.core_idea:
Iterative why questioning finds systemic causes beyond the immediate vulnerability — fix processes, not just patches.

Fishbone diagrams help for multifactor failures. Track corrective actions in risk register to verified closure.

children.title: IR Communication — Stakeholder Updates
children.label: IR Communication
children.summary: Scheduled updates to execs, legal, and customers — keep facts and assumptions clearly separated.
children.core_idea:
- Send updates on a fixed cadence (not just when something dramatic happens) so stakeholders aren't left guessing
- Clearly separate **confirmed facts** from **working assumptions** — speculation stated as fact erodes trust fast if it's later wrong
- Route all external statements (press, customers, regulators) through a single incident commander — no ad hoc comms from multiple people
- Preserve attorney-client privilege where applicable by looping legal in on written communications early, not after the fact

children.title: IR Legal & Regulatory Notification
children.label: IR Legal & Regulatory
children.summary: Breach notification laws (GDPR 72h, state US laws) have clocks — involve legal early to assess reporting obligations.
children.core_idea:
Breach notification laws (GDPR 72h, state US laws) have clocks — involve legal early to assess reporting obligations.

Document decision rationale if not notifying. Contractual notification to partners may be shorter than statutes.

children.title: IOC Sharing — ISACs & Threat Intel
children.label: IOC Sharing
children.summary: Share indicators with sector ISACs and vendors under NDA — consume peer reports to accelerate detection.
children.core_idea:
Share indicators with sector ISACs and vendors under NDA — consume peer reports to accelerate detection.

Normalize STIX/TAXII feeds. Tune detections on shared IOCs with expiration to avoid stale alerts.

children.title: IR Metrics — MTTD, MTTR, and Dwell Time
children.label: IR Metrics
children.summary: Mean time to detect/respond and attacker dwell time measure program maturity — trend quarterly, not vanity single incidents.
children.core_idea:
Mean time to detect/respond and attacker dwell time measure program maturity — trend quarterly, not vanity single incidents.

Segment by incident type. Pair with false-positive rate and tabletop participation for balanced scorecards.

children.title: Offensive Security
children.label: Offensive Security
children.summary: 15 notes across 2 section(s).

children.title: OSINT — Passive Reconnaissance Toolkit
children.label: OSINT
children.summary: OSINT works best when you combine passive public data with targeted active validation.
children.core_idea:
- Passive recon: websites, archived pages, public docs, job posts, social profiles.
- Active recon: controlled lookups and scans that may be logged by targets.
- Job listings and tech docs often leak stack versions and operating constraints.
- Archive/cache sources can expose content removed from current pages.
- Document findings by attack surface: identity, infra, apps, and third parties.

children.title: Nmap — Scanning Techniques Reference
children.label: Nmap
children.summary: Nmap is most effective when used in sequence: host discovery, service mapping, then targeted deep checks.
children.core_idea:
- Start with host discovery to separate alive targets from noise.
- Run port and service/version detection before vulnerability scripts.
- Adjust scan rate and scope to reduce operational risk and false alarms.
- Use results to build attack paths, not just open-port lists.
- Repeat after remediation to confirm exposure actually changed.

commands.explain: Stealth SYN scan with service/version detection, OS fingerprinting, and default scripts.
Skip host discovery and scan all 65535 ports — useful when ICMP is filtered.
Run NSE's vulnerability-detection script category against a target.

children.title: Shodan — Internet Asset Discovery
children.label: Shodan
children.summary: Shodan indexes banners and service metadata across the internet — useful for finding exposed ICS, RDP, and default-credential interfaces without touching the target directly.
children.core_idea:
Shodan continuously scans the internet and indexes what it finds — banners, service metadata, and (for many devices) default configuration fingerprints — letting you search that index rather than scanning yourself.

- Query by organization, product name, or known vulnerability tag
- Pair any Shodan-driven investigation with clear **legal scope** — you're searching a third party's index, but acting on what you find against a system you don't control still carries the same legal exposure as scanning it directly
- Complements active `nmap` scanning nicely: use Shodan to find exposed assets first, then run targeted active scans only against in-scope CIDR ranges

children.title: Google Dorking — Search Operator OSINT
children.label: Google Dorking
children.summary: Google dorks use search operators to discover exposed assets, files, and misconfigurations at scale.
children.core_idea:
- Use operators like site:, filetype:, intitle:, and inurl: to narrow exposure hunting.
- Focus on externally exposed data, not random query volume.
- Validate findings manually because indexing can be stale or false-positive.
- Use defensively: check what your own org exposes to public search.
- Treat discovered data as sensitive even if publicly indexed.

children.title: Buffer Overflow — Stack Layout
children.label: Buffer Overflow
children.summary: Overflowing a stack buffer can overwrite the saved return address — the classic path to arbitrary code execution before modern mitigations.
children.core_idea:
### Stack Layout (typical, growing downward)
```
[ buffer ] → [ saved EBP/RBP ] → [ saved return address ]
```
Writing past the end of `buffer` overwrites adjacent stack data — eventually reaching the saved return address, which lets an attacker redirect execution once the function returns.

### Modern Mitigations
- **ASLR** (Address Space Layout Randomization) — randomizes memory layout so an attacker can't reliably predict addresses
- **Stack canaries** — a known value placed before the return address; checked before returning, and if it's been clobbered by an overflow, execution is aborted
- **NX/DEP** (No-eXecute / Data Execution Prevention) — marks the stack non-executable, so injected shellcode can't simply run from the overflowed buffer

### Bypass Techniques
- **ROP (Return-Oriented Programming)** — chain existing executable code fragments instead of injecting new code, defeating NX
- **Info leaks** — separately leak a memory address to defeat ASLR, then combine with a controlled overwrite

children.title: ROP — Return-Oriented Programming
children.label: ROP
children.summary: Chaining existing code gadgets ending in `ret` lets an attacker execute arbitrary logic (like a syscall) even when NX blocks injected shellcode.
children.core_idea:
### Core Idea
Since NX/DEP prevents executing injected shellcode directly on the stack, ROP instead reuses tiny fragments of **already-executable** code ("gadgets") already present in the binary or its linked libraries — each gadget ends in a `ret` instruction, which pops the next gadget's address off the stack and jumps to it, chaining arbitrary sequences of operations.

### Typical Workflow
1. Find usable gadgets in the target binary and its loaded libraries
2. Chain them to set up arguments and call a useful function — commonly `mprotect` (to re-mark a memory region executable) or `execve` (to spawn a shell)
3. Point the corrupted return address at the start of the chain

### Defenses
- **CET (Control-flow Enforcement Technology)** — hardware-assisted shadow stack and indirect-branch tracking
- **Shadow stack** — a separate, protected copy of return addresses that can't be corrupted by a normal buffer overflow
- **High-entropy ASLR** — makes gadget addresses harder to locate reliably

children.title: Spectre & Meltdown — CPU Side Channels
children.label: Spectre & Meltdown
children.summary: Speculative execution can leak data across isolation boundaries via cache-timing side channels; mitigations trade performance for safety.
children.core_idea:
### The Core Issue
Modern CPUs speculatively execute instructions ahead of confirming they're actually needed, for performance. If a speculative path touches secret data before being rolled back, traces of that access can leak through **cache timing** — even though the speculative result itself is architecturally discarded.

### Meltdown
Lets an unprivileged user process **read kernel memory** by exploiting out-of-order execution that briefly accesses privileged memory before the permission check completes.

### Spectre
Tricks a *victim* process into speculatively executing code that accesses secret data conditioned on attacker-influenced branch prediction, then infers the secret via a cache-timing side channel — harder to fully patch since it exploits legitimate speculative execution rather than a specific implementation bug.

### Mitigations
- **KPTI (Kernel Page Table Isolation)** — separates kernel and user page tables to close the Meltdown-style read path
- **Retpoline** — a compiler technique that replaces indirect branches with a construct that resists speculative misprediction
- Microcode/OS patches for specific variants, generally at a measurable **performance cost**
- Strong isolation between mutually-untrusting workloads (e.g. separate physical hosts for sensitive multi-tenant VMs) reduces exposure where patch-level mitigation isn't enough

children.title: Metasploit Use: Power, Risk, and Scope
children.label: Metasploit Risk & Scope
children.summary: Metasploit accelerates exploitation workflows, so strict scope control and verification discipline are essential.
children.core_idea:
- Framework modules speed validation of known weaknesses.
- Automation can overshoot intent if targets and bounds are loose.
- Operator judgment is still required for safe exploitation choices.
- Use captured evidence and reproducible steps for reporting quality.
- Always align exploit activity with explicit rules of engagement.

children.title: Privilege Escalation via Unpatched Software
children.label: Privilege Escalation Paths
children.summary: Privilege escalation often succeeds by chaining initial access with unpatched OS or application flaws.
children.core_idea:
- Initial low-priv footholds are common; escalation unlocks broader impact.
- Local misconfig and vulnerable services create repeatable escalation paths.
- Patch lag and weak least-privilege controls are frequent root causes.
- Exploit attempts are noisy and should be constrained by agreed test scope.
- Defenders prioritize patch hygiene and privilege boundary hardening.

children.title: Command-Shell Backdoors (Netcat Pattern)
children.label: Command-Shell Backdoors
children.summary: Command-shell backdoors expose remote shell access and are commonly used to preserve post-exploitation control.
children.core_idea:
- Simple listener/client patterns can create unauthorized remote command access.
- Backdoor channels may run over nonstandard ports to evade casual checks.
- Persistence value is high for attackers and high-priority for responders.
- Defenders monitor anomalous listeners, process ancestry, and egress behavior.
- Remove artifacts and validate full cleanup after authorized testing.

children.title: Honeypots
children.label: Honeypots
children.summary: A honeypot is a deliberately vulnerable system with fake data, designed to attract attackers, waste their time, and generate high-confidence alerts.
children.core_idea:
### What Is a Honeypot?
A system left **intentionally vulnerable** — default settings, missing patches, known misconfigurations — with fake data planted on it to make it resemble a plausible, valuable target for an attacker.

### Why They Work
- No legitimate user has any reason to touch a honeypot, so **any interaction with it is a strong signal of malicious activity** — a very low false-positive detection source compared to production-network alerts
- They can absorb attacker time and effort that would otherwise be spent probing real assets
- Observed attacker behavior against a honeypot (tools, techniques, timing) feeds threat intelligence without risking real data

### Caveats
- A honeypot only helps if attackers actually find and engage with it — poorly placed or obviously fake honeypots provide no value
- Sophisticated attackers may fingerprint and avoid known honeypot signatures

children.title: Evil Twin / Rogue Access Point Attack
children.label: Evil Twin Attack
children.summary: An evil twin attack lures clients to a rogue AP that mimics a trusted wireless network.
children.core_idea:
- Attacker clones SSID and entices clients using stronger or more convenient signal.
- Victims route traffic through attacker-controlled infrastructure.
- Enables credential harvesting, traffic capture, and content manipulation.
- Operational success depends on client behavior and wireless controls in place.
- Defenses include rogue AP detection, certificate validation, and user training.

children.title: WEP Cracking (Legacy Risk)
children.label: WEP Cracking
children.summary: WEP is cryptographically weak and should be treated as deprecated legacy exposure, not modern protection.
children.core_idea:
- Weak IV handling enables key recovery with sufficient captured traffic.
- Packet-injection tactics can accelerate capture volume for key analysis.
- Practical security posture: any WEP-enabled network is high risk.
- Modern environments should use WPA2/WPA3 with strong auth.
- Use WEP only as a migration red-flag in assessments.

children.title: War Driving and Wireless Exposure Recon
children.label: War Driving
children.summary: War driving maps wireless exposure and identifies weakly secured networks from nearby physical space.
children.core_idea:
- Focus is discovery of SSIDs, encryption modes, and signal reach.
- Helps quantify unintended coverage and rogue-broadcast risk.
- Collected metadata supports prioritizing hardening and segmentation.
- May reveal default configurations and outdated security modes.
- Use ethically and only within authorized assessment boundaries.

children.title: Bluetooth Attack Families (Bluejacking/Bluesnarfing/etc.)
children.label: Bluetooth Attack Families
children.summary: Bluetooth attacks target discoverability, weak pairing trust, and insecure device exposure paths.
children.core_idea:
- Bluejacking pushes unsolicited messages; bluesnarfing steals data.
- Bluebugging/bluesmack patterns can enable control abuse or service disruption.
- Risk rises when devices remain discoverable or pair broadly by default.
- Mobile endpoints increase impact due to credential and messaging data.
- Defenses: non-discoverable defaults, strict pairing policy, and patch hygiene.

children.title: Malware & RE
children.label: Malware & RE
children.summary: 9 notes across 1 section(s).

children.title: Malware Taxonomy — Viruses, Worms, Trojans & Ransomware
children.label: Malware Taxonomy
children.summary: Malware families differ by propagation model, payload goal, and persistence mechanism.
children.core_idea:
- Trojans masquerade as benign software to deliver unauthorized capability.
- Backdoors preserve remote access after initial compromise.
- Worms self-propagate across reachable systems without direct user action.
- Viruses typically attach to host files and spread with execution.
- Classification helps prioritize containment and eradication steps.

children.title: CherryBlos — Mobile Banking Trojan Case Study
children.label: CherryBlos
children.summary: CherryBlos combined OCR-based credential theft (scanning photo galleries for crypto seed phrases) with Accessibility Service abuse to overlay fake screens on real banking apps.
children.core_idea:
### Background
Discovered by Trend Micro in mid-2023 (MITRE ATT&CK Software ID: **S1225**). A multi-stage Android malware family with an unusually creative theft mechanism.

### Objective
Direct financial theft, specifically targeting **cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases** rather than conventional data like emails or documents.

### OCR-Based Theft
CherryBlos used **Optical Character Recognition** to scan a victim's photo gallery for screenshots containing crypto wallet seed phrases. Despite repeated platform warnings against it, users commonly screenshot their recovery phrases during wallet setup — CherryBlos automated the search for these "digital master keys" across the entire gallery.

### Accessibility Service Abuse
The malware social-engineered victims into enabling Android's **Accessibility Services** (designed for users with disabilities), then abused those elevated permissions to auto-approve further permission requests and to **overlay fake login screens on top of real banking apps**, harvesting credentials as the victim typed them into what looked like the genuine app.

### Takeaway
A useful case study in how legitimate accessibility/OS features become high-value abuse targets once granted — and why "screenshot your recovery phrase" is specifically the kind of user habit malware authors design around.

children.title: Real-World Cyber-Physical Attack Case Studies
children.label: Real
children.summary: From Stuxnet to the Colonial Pipeline, these incidents show attackers moving from data theft into physical-world consequences.
children.core_idea:
| Incident | What Happened |
|---|---|
| **Target (2013)** | Attackers gained credentials via a compromised HVAC contractor, installed memory-scraping malware on POS terminals, and stole millions of credit card numbers |
| **Sony Pictures (2014)** | Believed to be an APT; entry point unclear. One of the first attacks to cause widespread destruction of computing resources, combining data theft with operational disruption |
| **Turkish Pipeline (2008)** | One of the earliest known cyber-physical attacks — gained access via internet-connected cameras, altered pipeline pressure settings, and disabled monitoring |
| **Iranian Centrifuges — Stuxnet** | Malware manipulated centrifuge sensor data to cause physical damage while reporting normal readings to operators — exploited process-level vulnerabilities, not just IT ones |
| **Ukraine Power Grid** | Russian-attributed attack causing widespread power outages |
| **Colonial Pipeline (2021)** | Ransomware disrupted business IT systems severely enough to halt fuel distribution across the U.S. East Coast, despite the ransomware itself not touching OT/pipeline control systems directly |
| **Florida Water Treatment Plant (2021)** | Attacker gained remote access and attempted to raise sodium hydroxide (lye) to dangerous concentrations |
| **2016 DNC Email Leak** | Spear phishing led to leaked emails that influenced public opinion during a presidential election — an influence-goal attack, not a financial one |
| **2020 Twitter Bitcoin Scam** | Insiders were social-engineered into granting access to high-profile verified accounts, used to run a cryptocurrency scam at scale |

**Pattern:** the highest-consequence incidents (Stuxnet, Florida, Ukraine, Colonial Pipeline) all involve crossing from the IT domain into physical/OT consequences — the common thread worth remembering when scoping "worst case" for critical infrastructure.

children.title: Static vs Dynamic Malware Analysis
children.label: Static vs Dynamic Malware
children.summary: Static and dynamic analysis complement each other for faster, safer malware triage.
children.core_idea:
- Static analysis inspects binaries without execution to extract indicators and intent.
- Dynamic analysis observes runtime behavior, network calls, and persistence actions.
- File-integrity monitoring helps detect unauthorized post-compromise changes.
- Use isolated sandboxes to limit analyst and infrastructure risk.
- Cross-validate indicators between static artifacts and runtime telemetry.

children.title: YARA — Pattern Matching for Malware
children.label: YARA
children.summary: YARA rules match strings, hex patterns, or regex with boolean conditions, letting you scan files, memory, or traffic for malware signatures at scale.
children.core_idea:
### Rule Structure
```
rule ExampleRule {
    meta:
        author = "analyst"
        description = "..."
    strings:
        $s1 = "malicious_string"
        $hex1 = { E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? }
    condition:
        $s1 or $hex1
}
```
- **meta** — free-form metadata, not evaluated
- **strings** — text, hex byte patterns (with wildcards `??`), or regex to search for
- **condition** — boolean logic over the defined strings (`and`/`or`/counts/`all of them`)

Use the built-in **`pe` module** for structural PE-header conditions (imports, sections, entry point) instead of relying purely on byte patterns.

### Practice
Always test a new rule against a large corpus of **known-clean** files to measure its false-positive rate before deploying it in a detection pipeline.

commands.explain: Scan a file or directory against a YARA rule.
Recursively scan a directory tree.

children.title: Cyber-Enabled Adversary Goals — Money, Data, Disruption, Influence
children.label: Cyber
children.summary: Adversary goals cluster into five categories — money, data, disruption, influence, and public trust — and are frequently pursued together.
children.core_idea:
| Goal | Mechanisms |
|---|---|
| **Money** | Direct theft (account takeover, redirecting funds, purchase fraud), ransomware, extortion |
| **Data** | PII, medical records, IP, and operational/infrastructure plans — targeted for disclosure, reuse (identity theft, account access), or as a stepping stone toward a larger attack; can also be held hostage |
| **Disruption** | Physical services (power, water, traffic, gas, building controls, medical devices) or IT services (911 systems, government services, communications) — used either as ransom leverage or as the end goal itself (terror/chaos) |
| **Influence** | Personal (swatting, fake kidnapping claims, direct threats — usually paired with a money demand) or public (aimed purely at fear/chaos, not necessarily financial gain) |
| **Public Trust** | Eroding confidence in governments, elected officials, public services, elections, or corporate brands |

These goals are rarely pursued in isolation — a ransomware attack, for example, simultaneously chases **money** (extortion) and **disruption** (as the leverage that makes the extortion work).

children.title: MITRE ATT&CK — Tactic & Technique Mapping
children.label: MITRE ATT&CK
children.summary: Mapping observed behaviors to standardized ATT&CK tactics/techniques gives detection engineering and incident reporting a common, comparable vocabulary.
children.core_idea:
### Why Map to ATT&CK
Translating raw observed behavior ("this process spawned that process and reached out to this IP") into standardized **tactic/technique IDs** makes findings comparable across incidents, tools, and organizations — instead of every report using ad hoc language for the same underlying behavior.

### Practical Uses
- Reference specific **technique IDs** inside detection rules (e.g. Sigma rules) so a rule's coverage is self-documenting
- **Detection gap analysis** — plot which techniques your current detections actually cover, and where the blind spots are
- **ATT&CK Navigator layers** — visualize coverage (or an adversary's known technique set, like CherryBlos's Software ID S1225 above) as a heatmap over the full matrix, making gaps and overlaps immediately visible

children.title: Browser Lock / Tech Support Scams
children.label: Browser Lock / Tech
children.summary: A malicious page traps the browser with a loud fake infection warning and a support number, pressuring victims into paying for fictitious remediation.
children.core_idea:
### How It Works
1. **Trigger** — victim visits a compromised or intentionally malicious website
2. **Scare tactic** — a pop-up (often with an alarming auto-playing voice) claims the computer is infected with a virus or ransomware
3. **Lockdown effect** — the browser becomes unresponsive, or the pop-up reappears in a loop, creating the illusion the machine is genuinely locked
4. **Urgency & payment** — the message pushes the victim to call a "tech support" number immediately, where they're pressured into paying for fake remediation (or granting remote access that enables real compromise)

### Why It Works
Combines urgency, authority framing (fake Microsoft/Apple branding), and a plausible-sounding threat to override a typical user's usual caution — the browser lock itself is just a UI trick (a JavaScript loop or fullscreen overlay), not an actual infection, but victims rarely realize that in the moment.

### Mitigation
- User education: a real OS/AV infection alert never asks you to call a phone number
- Force-close via task manager rather than interacting with the page at all
- Keep browsers patched — some variants pair the social-engineering lock with an actual exploit attempt

children.title: Business Email Compromise (BEC) — Mechanics & Defense
children.label: Business Email Compromise
children.summary: BEC/EAC drive over 60% of data-loss incidents — layered technology, training, and out-of-band verification are the real defense.
children.core_idea:
- Social engineering is behind an estimated 60%+ of data-loss incidents; **BEC** targets businesses, **EAC** targets individuals with the same playbook
- **Entry point 1**: compromise a real account (phishing/password guessing), then *groom* the victim before making the actual ask — jumping straight to the fraudulent request raises suspicion
- **Entry point 2**: fabricate a new relationship — spoofed email/caller ID/text impersonating a bank or partner
- **Mitigation layers**: technology (DMARC/SPF/DKIM, external-sender tagging), user education (continuous, not annual), and process (verified out-of-band approval for any money transfer — no single email authorizes a payment alone)

children.title: Cryptography
children.label: Cryptography
children.summary: 12 notes across 1 section(s).

children.title: Cryptography Fundamentals — Symmetric, Asymmetric & Hashing
children.label: Cryptography Fundamentals
children.summary: Crypto choices should map to confidentiality, integrity, and authentication requirements by data flow.
children.core_idea:
- Symmetric crypto is fast for bulk data; asymmetric crypto solves key exchange and trust.
- Block vs stream cipher behavior matters for protocol design and misuse risks.
- Hashes provide integrity checks, not reversible encryption.
- Non-repudiation requires sound key management, not signatures alone.
- Weak/legacy primitives create breakable trust even in modern systems.

children.title: AES — GCM vs CBC Mode
children.label: AES
children.summary: GCM provides authenticated encryption (AEAD) in one step; CBC needs a separate MAC and is vulnerable to padding-oracle attacks if implemented incorrectly.
children.core_idea:
### CBC (Cipher Block Chaining)
Encrypts sequentially, each block XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption. Provides confidentiality only — **integrity/authentication must be added separately** (encrypt-then-MAC). Implementations that skip this, or that leak padding-validity information, are vulnerable to **padding oracle attacks**, which can let an attacker decrypt ciphertext without the key.

### GCM (Galois/Counter Mode)
An **AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data)** mode — provides confidentiality and integrity/authenticity in a single pass, with no separate MAC step needed.

### Practical Guidance
- Prefer **AES-GCM** or **ChaCha20-Poly1305** over CBC for new designs
- **Never reuse a nonce/IV with the same key under GCM** — doing so catastrophically breaks both confidentiality and authenticity for every message that shares the reused nonce

children.title: PKI — Public Key Infrastructure & X.509 Certificates
children.label: PKI
children.summary: PKI binds identities to public keys so encryption and signatures can be trusted at scale.
children.core_idea:
- Certificates assert subject identity through a CA trust chain.
- Validation must include issuer trust, expiry, and revocation state.
- Digital signatures support authenticity and non-repudiation claims.
- Compromised CAs or private keys collapse trust regardless of algorithm strength.
- Operational hygiene (issuance, rotation, revocation) is core PKI security.

children.title: TLS Handshake & Certificate Validation
children.label: TLS Handshake & Certificate
children.summary: The client verifies the server's certificate chain to a trusted CA, checks the hostname, validity period, and revocation status, then negotiates a cipher suite and session keys.
children.core_idea:
### Certificate Validation Steps
1. Verify the presented certificate chains up to a **trusted root CA**
2. Check the **hostname** against the certificate's Subject Alternative Name (SAN)
3. Confirm the certificate is within its **validity period**
4. Check **revocation status** (CRL or OCSP)

### Handshake
Negotiates the cipher suite and establishes session keys used for the rest of the connection — the actual bulk data transfer then uses fast symmetric encryption, with the handshake having handled key agreement asymmetrically (same hybrid pattern as PGP).

### Hardening Notes
- **Certificate pinning** mitigates the risk of a rogue/compromised CA issuing a fraudulent certificate for your domain, at the cost of needing careful pin rotation
- Monitor for and disable legacy protocol versions (**TLS 1.0/1.1**) still being negotiated — a sign of outdated clients or a permissive server configuration

children.title: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) — Hybrid Encryption Flow
children.label: PGP
children.summary: PGP combines symmetric and asymmetric encryption: a fast symmetric session key encrypts the message itself, and the recipient's public key encrypts just that session key.
children.core_idea:
### Why Hybrid?
Asymmetric encryption is computationally expensive for large messages; symmetric encryption is fast but needs a securely-shared key. PGP gets both: use symmetric encryption for the bulk data, and asymmetric encryption only for the small session key.

### Encryption Flow
1. Sender generates a random **symmetric session key**
2. The session key encrypts the actual message
3. The session key itself is encrypted with the **recipient's public key**
4. Both the encrypted message and the encrypted session key are sent together

### Decryption Flow
1. Recipient uses their **private key** to decrypt the session key
2. The recovered session key decrypts the message

This same pattern (asymmetric-wraps-symmetric) underlies TLS session establishment and most modern hybrid cryptosystems.

children.title: Kerberos — Trusted Third-Party Authentication
children.label: Kerberos
children.summary: Kerberos (MIT Project Athena, now v5) exchanges session keys via tickets issued by a trusted KDC, so passwords are never sent over the network after initial setup.
children.core_idea:
### Design Goals
- No plaintext passwords ever sent over the network
- No plaintext passwords stored on the KDC (Key Distribution Center)
- Passwords kept in memory only as briefly as possible
- Compromise of one user's session doesn't compromise others
- Tickets have a finite lifetime, bounding exposure
- Transparent to the end user, with minimal changes required to applications

### Key Terminology
- **Principal** — any Kerberos participant (user, client program, or server), named `primary_name.instance@REALM` (e.g. `jones@IASTATE.EDU`)
- **Realm** — the administrative domain (e.g. `IASTATE.EDU`)
- **Instance** — usually empty; can denote an elevated role (`root`, `admin`)

### Server Components
- **AS (Authentication Server)** — holds the user database; issues **TGTs (Ticket Granting Tickets)**
- **TGS (Ticket Granting Server)** — exchanges a valid TGT for a **service ticket** scoped to a specific resource

### Authentication Flow
1. User authenticates to the AS → receives a **TGT**
2. User presents the TGT to the TGS → receives a **service ticket** for the specific resource they want
3. User presents the service ticket to the target application/server → granted access

### Active Directory Integration
AD uses Kerberos to issue both a TGT and a session ("service") ticket, then hands off to an **X.500-style directory service** to manage user and application information for the remainder of the session.

### Common Attacks
- **Kerberoasting** — request service tickets for accounts with weak passwords, then crack the encrypted portion offline
- **AS-REP Roasting** — target accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, allowing an attacker to request an AS-REP without knowing the password first
- **Golden Ticket** — forge a TGT after compromising the KDC's master (`krbtgt`) key, granting persistent domain-wide access
- **Pass-the-Ticket** — reuse a stolen valid ticket directly, without ever needing the underlying password

children.title: Authentication Technologies — Key Cards, Smart Cards & S/Key
children.label: Authentication Technologies
children.summary: Hardware tokens range from PIN-activated key cards to smart cards with onboard storage, plus the older S/Key one-time password scheme built on a hash chain.
children.core_idea:
### Key Cards
PIN-activated, using either **asynchronous** (challenge/response) or **synchronous** (time-based) generation. Time-based cards need the verifying host to accept a small window of valid codes to tolerate clock drift. Typically allow only 3 attempts before lockout.

### Smart Cards
A physical card with a direct electrical/contact interface (inserted into a reader), authenticated by PIN or fingerprint, and capable of storing significantly more data than a simple key card. Generally considered more secure than key cards.

### One-Time Passwords — S/Key (Bell Labs)
Designed for users authenticating from untrusted networks (e.g. travelers outside the corporate perimeter). Built on a **one-way hash chain**:
```
P1 = hash(password)
P2 = hash(P1)
P3 = hash(P2)
...
```
Only the **last** key in the chain is stored server-side. The user authenticates by presenting keys in *reverse* order — each one is verified against the currently-stored value and then replaces it. Since each key is used exactly once and the hash chain can't be run forward from a captured value, this is far more resistant to replay than a static password.

children.title: Password Storage & Offline Cracking
children.label: Password Storage & Offline
children.summary: Password security depends on strong hashing, salting, and resistance to offline cracking workflows.
children.core_idea:
- Attackers prefer offline cracking after obtaining password hashes.
- Dictionary, hybrid, and brute-force attacks trade speed vs coverage.
- Salts prevent precomputed rainbow-table reuse across accounts.
- Legacy hash choices and short passwords drastically reduce crack time.
- Defenders combine strong KDFs, MFA, lockouts, and credential hygiene.

children.title: Host, User & Application-Layer Authentication
children.label: Host, User & Application
children.summary: Host-to-host trust ranked weakest (bare IP/hostname) to strongest (signed + encrypted + trusted third party); user-to-user and host-to-user both ultimately rely on some form of public key trust.
children.core_idea:
### Host-to-Host Authentication
Underpins firewalls, IDS, backup systems, and network filesystem mounting. Ranked weakest to strongest:
1. **No authentication / bare IP or hostname** — trivially spoofed, not real authentication at all
2. **Password-based** — only marginally stronger
3. **Digital signatures + encryption + a trusted third party** — the recommended approach

### User-to-User Authentication
Relies on digital signatures and public key cryptography — the same primitives used for host-to-user auth, just applied between two end users directly (e.g. signed/encrypted email).

### Host-to-User Authentication
Relies on digital certificates (HTTPS server certificates), digital signatures (common in signed software distribution), and public key encryption. In every case, the chain of trust ultimately bottoms out at some trusted source — a CA, a known public key, or a trusted third party like a KDC.

children.title: Authentication Failure Category — Implementation & Deployment
children.label: Authentication Failure Category
children.summary: A cryptographically sound protocol deployed badly is just as broken as a weak one — configuration errors dominate real-world breaches more than algorithm flaws.
children.core_idea:
Even a secure protocol fails in practice if deployed carelessly:
- **Misconfigured TLS** — weak/deprecated cipher suites still enabled, or improper certificate validation (accepting invalid/self-signed certs without warning)
- **Overprivileged service accounts** combined with poor password hygiene on those accounts
- **Long-lived tokens** that, once stolen, amplify how long an attacker can persist

**Mitigations:** regular configuration audits, enforcing least privilege, hardened secure-by-default configurations, and continuous (not one-time) validation of deployed settings.

children.title: Data Loss Prevention — Key Questions & the Five C's
children.label: Data Loss Prevention
children.summary: DLP requires knowing where data lives, who controls it, and covering data at rest, in motion, and on devices — organized around five practical C's.
children.core_idea:
### Key DLP Questions
- Where is your data located? (centralized, distributed, or both)
- Who has access, and at what level (read/write/delete)?
- Who actually **controls** it — owners, general users, or effectively anyone?
- Are you covering **data at rest**, **data in motion**, *and* **data on devices** — or just one of the three?

### Three States of Data
| State | Concerns |
|---|---|
| **At rest** | Data is stored somewhere, often in more places than intended — discovery (finding where it all lives) and protection (encryption, device locking) are both hard |
| **In motion** | Preventing sensitive data (SSNs, account numbers, records) from leaving the organization — DLP tooling can log, block, or encrypt violating traffic; requires visibility into which protocols and (often unsanctioned) applications are moving data |
| **On devices** | Do people carry data on phones/laptops/tablets? Do they remotely access it from mobile devices? Every device that can touch the data expands the loss surface |

### The Five C's of Data Protection
| # | C | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Classification** | Build a taxonomy of data types and assign protection levels to each |
| 2 | **Compartmentalization** | Control who has access to what, limiting blast radius |
| 3 | **Cryptography** | Encrypt data at rest, in motion, and on devices |
| 4 | **Contingency Planning** | Plan for data loss *before* it happens, not after |
| 5 | **Coaching** | Train everyone — technical controls fail without user buy-in |

children.title: Governance/Risk/Compliance
children.label: Governance/Risk/Compliance
children.summary: No content yet — reserved for future notes.

children.title: Compliance Frameworks at a Glance — NIST CSF, ISO 27001, SOC 2
children.label: Compliance Frameworks
children.summary: NIST CSF is a risk-management guide, ISO 27001 is a certifiable ISMS standard, SOC 2 proves controls to customers.
children.core_idea:
- **NIST CSF** — voluntary risk-management framework, organized around Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover — not itself certifiable
- **ISO 27001** — internationally recognized, certifiable Information Security Management System (ISMS) standard — requires an external audit
- **SOC 2** — attestation report (Type I = point-in-time, Type II = over a period) proving controls to customers/partners, common in SaaS sales cycles
- These aren't mutually exclusive — many orgs map controls once and satisfy multiple frameworks from the same evidence

children.title: Risk Register Basics
children.label: Risk Register
children.summary: A living log of identified risks, their likelihood/impact, owner, and treatment plan.
children.core_idea:
- Each entry: risk description, likelihood, impact, current controls, residual risk, owner, treatment plan, review date
- **Treatment options**: accept, mitigate, transfer (e.g. insurance), avoid — pick deliberately, don't default to "mitigate everything"
- Residual risk (after controls) is what actually gets tracked and reported to leadership — not the raw, uncontrolled risk
- Needs a named owner and review cadence, or it becomes a stale document nobody revisits after the initial risk assessment

children.title: Third-Party / Vendor Risk Management
children.label: Vendor Risk
children.summary: A vendor's security posture becomes your risk the moment they touch your data or systems.
children.core_idea:
- Assess vendors *before* onboarding (security questionnaires, SOC 2 reports, pen test summaries) — not after a breach reveals the gap
- Tier vendors by data sensitivity/access level — a payroll processor needs deeper scrutiny than a marketing analytics tool
- Contract terms matter: breach notification timelines, right-to-audit clauses, data handling/deletion requirements
- Ongoing monitoring, not one-time approval — a vendor's posture can degrade well after the initial review

children.title: Compliance Drivers by Industry — PCI-DSS, HIPAA, GDPR
children.label: Compliance by Industry
children.summary: The applicable regulation depends on data type and geography, not company size.
children.core_idea:
- **PCI-DSS** — anyone storing/processing/transmitting cardholder data; scope shrinks dramatically if you tokenize/outsource card handling
- **HIPAA** — covers Protected Health Information (PHI) for healthcare providers, insurers, and their business associates
- **GDPR** — applies to any org processing EU residents' personal data, regardless of where the company itself is based
- Regulation drives specific technical requirements (encryption, breach notification windows, data subject rights) — know which ones actually apply before designing controls around all of them

children.title: Vulnerability Assessment vs Penetration Test
children.label: VA vs Pentest
children.summary: A vulnerability assessment finds weaknesses; a penetration test validates exploitability and business impact.
children.core_idea:
- VA emphasizes breadth and inventory of known issues.
- Pentest emphasizes realistic attack paths and demonstrated risk.
- Both are complementary and should feed remediation planning.
- Method choice depends on objective, scope, and operational tolerance.
- Reporting should separate confirmed exploit paths from theoretical findings.

children.title: Penetration Test Scope and Rules of Engagement
children.label: Pentest Scope & ROE
children.summary: Clear scope and rules of engagement prevent unsafe testing and align technical execution with business constraints.
children.core_idea:
- Define in-scope assets, prohibited actions, and escalation contacts up front.
- Document legal authorization and confidentiality obligations before testing.
- Specify stop conditions for operational or safety risk.
- Align evidence collection and cleanup expectations before kickoff.
- Good ROE reduces ambiguity during high-pressure incident-like moments.

children.title: SIEM Platforms — Splunk vs Sentinel vs QRadar
children.label: SIEM Comparison
children.summary: Splunk is the flexible/expensive industry standard; Sentinel is cloud-native and Azure-integrated; QRadar is on-prem-strong, enterprise-heavy.
children.core_idea:
- **Splunk** — most flexible query language (SPL), huge community/app ecosystem, but licensing cost scales fast with data volume
- **Microsoft Sentinel** — cloud-native, deeply integrated with Azure/M365 signals, consumption-based pricing, KQL query language
- **IBM QRadar** — strong in on-prem/hybrid enterprise environments, mature correlation rule engine, steeper learning curve
- Interview framing: know the query language name for each (SPL, KQL) and that "which SIEM" matters less than understanding log sources, correlation rules, and alert tuning

children.title: EDR Platforms — CrowdStrike, Defender, SentinelOne
children.label: EDR Comparison
children.summary: All three do endpoint detection/response; differences are in AI-driven autonomous response and deployment model.
children.core_idea:
- **CrowdStrike Falcon** — cloud-native, lightweight agent, strong threat-intel integration, market leader in enterprise EDR
- **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** — deeply integrated with Windows/M365, strong value if already on the Microsoft stack
- **SentinelOne** — emphasizes autonomous, AI-driven response (can auto-remediate without waiting for analyst action)
- All three share the core EDR loop: telemetry collection → behavioral detection → alert/auto-response → forensic timeline for the analyst

children.title: SOAR & Ticketing Basics
children.label: SOAR & Ticketing
children.summary: SOAR automates repetitive response steps; ticketing tracks the human workflow around each incident.
children.core_idea:
- **SOAR** (Security Orchestration, Automation & Response) — runs playbooks that automate repetitive triage steps (e.g. auto-enrich an IP, auto-quarantine a host)
- Reduces analyst time on low-value repetitive tasks so they can focus on judgment calls
- **Ticketing** (Jira, ServiceNow) — tracks the incident lifecycle, ownership, SLAs, and audit trail of who did what and when
- SOAR and ticketing are usually integrated — a SOAR playbook creates/updates the ticket automatically as it runs
